utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, how do you feel today? Do you feel one year older?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: My actual birthday was already last Saturday so I feel one year and three days older, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am with you, only it is probably three years and one day! OK. You may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. I will just first briefly summarise where I went yesterday. I started referring to the decision of the Appeals Chamber, especially where the Appeals Chamber decided that the clashes between the rebel forces and the central government forces would only result in an international armed conflict if the Bosnian Serb forces would have to be regarded as organs or agents of Belgrade. This is the language of both the Appeals Chamber and the International Court of Justice in the Nicaragua case, dependance and control, control to such a degree in all fields that it would justify to equate the Bosnian Serbs, for legal purposes, with an organ or agents of Belgrade. I also pointed at the circumstances that would not allow to reconstruct the organisation, equipment, personnel and supplies of the Bosnian Serb forces. I now come to a question raised twice by you, Judge McDonald, a question of state responsibility. The question of state responsibility has first to be answered in order to establish whether the armed conflict was of an international character. That is important, since Article 2 of the Statute requires the existence of such an international conflict before we can enter the area of individual responsibility for the grave breaches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you this? I suppose the armed conflict, as far as Hambarine, as far as Prijedor was concerned, would have occurred before the withdrawal of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That was clearly, I suppose, an international armed conflict ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there has been ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- and why does it not continue until peace is ultimately arrived at?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think if we look at what happened in these times, there was the declaration of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Almost immediately afterwards we had a declaration of independence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The actual situation at that time was that the JNA was still there and I would say the international character of the conflict derived more from what happened before in Croatia and what happened before. At that moment we were in a state of transition. On from 19th May, I think, it became clear that the JNA would withdraw and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be an independent state at that moment. So it is that period of transition. I would say that it was both the end of the international conflict and the beginning of the internal conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But what ended the international conflict? There was no peace?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: There was no peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I thought it continued in the absence of some conclusion of peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would say that it was converted at that time in an internal conflict, your Honour. Going back to the decision of the International Court of Justice in the Nicaragua case, the International Court of Justice -- I am trying to seek the criteria to be used -- decided that the United States participation, even if preponderant or decisive, in the financial, training, supplying and equipping of the Contras, the selection of its military and paramilitary targets, and the planning of the whole of its operation was still insufficient in itself for the purpose of attributing to the United States responsibility of what the Contras had done. That is paragraph 114 of the decision on the merits in the Nicaragua case of June 27th 1986. It is our submission that the Prosecution has been far away from proving a situation of involvement of the Belgrade government that went any further than the US involvement in Nicaragua. Even in the testimony of Dr. Gow, which has struck the Defence by being very one-sided, one cannot find anything more than the actual leaving behind of equipment, armoury and officers and soldiers while the JNA was split up. Being asked whether the spring offensive in 1992 was a planned operation by the JNA, Dr. Gow answered that the operations in the spring of 1992 were planned and co-ordinated actions, involving elements of the JNA. The question was whether it was a planned operation by the JNA. He said it was planned and co-ordinated involving elements of the JNA, apart from that also local Serbian Territorial Defence units and paramilitary groups. That was even before the split up and the withdrawal of the JNA. In cross-examination, Dr. Gow testified that it is difficult to say what JNA means after 19th May. He still considers that the remainings of the JNA to be elements of the JNA. That is the second example I promised you of how witnesses and experts would use the word "JNA" even after the split up of the JNA and VRS and the army of the federation. So he still considered the remainings of the JNA to be elements of the JNA, even when the arms, equipment and people were integrated in the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So whenever he uses the word "JNA" or "elements of the JNA", one should ask oneself what he actually meant to say, since his explanation demonstrates that he might well have meant the remaining parts of the JNA on Bosnia and Herzegovina territory, then called the VRS. This is not surprising since Dr. Gow considers whatever facts in the light of what he sees as General Kadijevic's master plan. Every single event must fit into that master plan. New developments just are ignored when they do not fit in. Dr. Gow also testified in cross-examination that the Bosnian presidency, even into May 1992, sought to achieve some kind of an arrangement with the local command of the JNA and that they actually co-operated in joint patrols. Negotiations were ongoing as to whether the JNA and Bosnia and Herzegovina would be the backbone of the new Bosnian and Herzegovina army. Dr. Gow did not exclude the possibility that General Mladic took his decisions already at that time against what Belgrade (that was still responsible for the withdrawal of the JNA) wished him to do. He was reluctant to admit those facts since they did not fit into his interpretation of what the greater Serbian idea was about, neither did the competing nationalistic ideas fit into his interpretation. Similar testimony has been given by Colonel Selak. He is very clear where he testifies that on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina (or, rather, the Republika Srpska), there was only one army, and that was the army of the Republika Srpska, as he says on page 1249. He confirms that there was no formal chain of command between the VRS and the VJ, page 1259. The chain of command was from the regions to the VRS command, the same page. It was the main staff that commanded the units and bases. Even if communication equipment would be technically going through Belgrade, telephone conversations of Colonel Selak and General Dukic took place while the latter was actually in Pale, not in Belgrade. When explaining the dotted lines on the charts, Colonel Selak explains that there was no real -- he is not talking about formal -- chain of command, although, in fact, there was co-ordination between the main staff of the VRS and the VJ, but no other relations were really existing. Similar testimony has also been given by Colonel Kranjc. He has told us that operations such as the operation in the Sava Valley corridor were ordered by the main staff of the army of the Republika Srpska on page 1320. The Corps command was reporting to the VRS command headquarters. On a more practical level, Colonel Selak has testified that the tanks and APCs that were used in the attack on Kozarac were under the control of the military of the VRS. Only the Corps Commander could give approval for the use of brigades for the attack on Kozarac, pages 1284 and 85. Apart from financial support (paying the officers), for example, the acceptance that remaining equipment, buildings etc. would be used by the VRS in the future (part of the equipment was taken into Serbia proper), no evidence has been presented to the extent that the FRY government or military were planning, let alone controlling, the operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, the criteria of the International Court of Justice in the Nicaragua case, and I repeat it, such a degree of control in all fields as to justify for legal purposes treating the Bosnian Serbs as acting on behalf of the Belgrade government has not been met in the relevant time. These findings are not surprising, not only the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina had collapsed in 1991 and early 1992, as has been extensively told to us by Professor Hayden, but also the JNA was in a state of dissolution. Various witnesses have testified and documentary evidence has shown that most of the officers and soldiers of the JNA in Bosnia were already at that time of Bosnian origin. Therefore, only some 20 per cent of the people in the withdrawing JNA felt that they were going home while withdrawing to Serbia and Montenegro. The two incidents that have been invoked by the Prosecution could not possibly change this conclusion. The first incident is contained in the testimony of Mr. Tihic. He was brought by helicopter to the territory of Serbia proper. This was only shortly after the declaration of independence. That incident started late in April 1992, far before the relevant time, that is the date of withdrawal of the JNA. The actual transfer by helicopter was effected by one of Arkan's men, a military, and another civilian. That is on page 8974. Repeatedly, the Prosecution has spoken about the JNA helicopter. That is not what the testimony of Mr. Tihic says. He talks about a helicopter. Even within Serbian territory, the paramilitary seemed initially to be in control, and the mere fact that Mr. Tihic was later detained in a police station within Serbia is not such as to be of major importance for the classification of the conflict. The second event referred to by the Prosecutor are the observations of Mr. Vulliamy of what happened in Loznica, a detention camp close to the border. Where he talks about running a camp by Serbian police, he immediately adds that this was on Serbian territory, unlike other places he talked about that were situated in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He also describes the situation in Zepa near that border, where he sees military traffic crossing the border in either way. He did not see any heavy tanks or anything, but there were some small armoured vehicles crossing. Having been asked whether these soldiers, regardless of the insignia, appeared to act as one unit, he replies that there was no reason to believe that they were not. How he could draw this conclusion when describing soldiers doing some casual patrolling and attaching flags to lampposts is still unexplainable for someone who was there only for a short period of time. That he also saw car maintenance done and that soldiers would even have their evening drinks at the other side of the border does not justify either the conclusion that the FRY was controlling to such a degree the operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina as to equate the Bosnian Serbs acting on behalf of the Belgrade government. The overall picture that has been established, that the presence of the JNA after the declaration of independence and the quick recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, gave rise to a rivalry between the central government and the Bosnian Serb leadership to take control of the remaining parts of the JNA. Forces of the central government, at least forces under their control, would forcibly obstruct the withdrawal if they feared that the remaining arms and equipment of the JNA might fall into the hands of Bosnian Serbs. Withdrawal was not complete to the extent that only a smaller part of the officers and soldiers originating from Serbia and Montenegro had returned to the territory of the Federation, and that some others wanted to stay for personal reasons. At that time they felt not bound any more by decisions taken in Belgrade since they regarded themselves troops of the newly created army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the VRS. Furthermore, the withdrawal was hindered while a free way out to Serbia and Montenegro was blocked, very often caused by the presence of enemy forces on their way. Apart, perhaps, from one isolated remark by Mr. Doko, not very much specified, none of the experts and witnesses of the Prosecution have clearly established that after 19th May the former elements of the JNA were following instructions from Belgrade, nor that any instructions were given by Belgrade, apart from the order to withdraw. The new instructions sprang from the Pale government, and whatever dotted lines may have been drawn in the Exhibits between Pale and Belgrade they have not been substantiated in the testimonies that have been given. The Appeals Chamber has indicated that the characterisation of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, other than an internal one, would lead to an absurd outcome. The underlining thought is that Bosnian Serbs would not be protected persons under Geneva Convention IV. Bosnian Serbs would have had the option of retaining their SFRY nationality, or otherwise adopting the nationality of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That is what the answer of the Prosecution is to that issue. I think that response that they could have opted for another nationality is even more absurd than the absurdity the Appeals Chamber talks about. Let us just for argument sake take this line of thinking seriously. We would then find that, on the basis of the treaties invoked by the Prosecutor, the Bosnian Muslims would have had the same option to change their nationality. No evidence whatsoever has been presented that one single Bosnian, whether Serb or Muslim, has made this choice. It would also implicate that the Prosecution would have to prove that all victims of the crimes charged had not made such an option, such a choice, for another nationality. In this absurd line of thought, it was far from sure that they were still holding the nationality of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is, therefore, a purely hypothetical construction, not a realistic approach. This becomes even more clear if we look at the legal instruments mentioned by the Prosecution. Article 10 of the convention on the reduction of statelessness takes as the starting point that provisions should be adopted whenever territory is transferred to another state in order to prevent citizens to become stateless. No treaty was concluded when Bosnia and Herzegovina declared its independence. Under these circumstances, Article 10, paragraph 2, would apply, providing the citizenship of the new state for all those who would otherwise become stateless. It is obvious that the majority of the Bosnian Serbs would regard themselves as citizens of the newly established Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the spring of 1992. This is emphasised by the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was only adopted under the Dayton Agreement in 1995. It provides that no persons shall be deprived of not only the citizenship of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also not of the entity citizenship arbitrarily or so as to leave him or her stateless. That realistically reflects the situation where Bosnian Serbs considered themselves citizens of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and since December 1992 of the Republika Srspka. If it would be true that a substantive number of Bosnian Serbs would not legally have obtained the Bosnian and Herzegovinan citizenship at the time of the declaration of independence, or would massively have opted for SFRY or RFY citizenship immediately thereafter, this would have meant that one of the elementary constituent elements of the newly established Republic as a state would have been missing, and that is a people. Precipitous recognition of such a state would be in violation of the sovereign rights of the Socialist Federal Republic. Even if I might be inclined to take that position, that it was a precipitous recognition, I certainly think that the Prosecution would not accept such a consequence. I would take that position because of the unconstitutionality of the process of getting to the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I refer to the statements of Professor Hayden. I explained that under Article 10, paragraph 2, of the convention on the reduction of statelessness, there was no question of the nationality of Bosnian Serbs, nor of Bosnian Croats or Muslims, being indeterminate as an alternative. But if this would be the case, then there is no basis in international customary law to expand the scope of "protected persons". No authority has been provided by the Prosecutor for such a solution. The consequence then would be that the citizenship of all other ethnic groups in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, more especially, in areas where the majority of the population was Serbian, would be just as indeterminate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Would be indeterminate, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is the last option the Prosecution has taken in its pretrial brief on it might have been indeterminate, and that would be valid for all the other groups as well. I come to a conclusion, your Honours. In the relevant time, say, after or perhaps shortly before 19th May, but I will say after 19th May 1992, the conflict in the opstina Prijedor was of an internal character and, therefore, the Tribunal has no jurisdiction over any of the grave breach charges, that might be the same acts as charged under Article 3 or Article 5 of the Statute, but no jurisdiction over the grave breach charges, or that at least the defendant should be acquitted on those charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, when you say it would be internal, internal as between citizens of Bosnia Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Armed forces, whether or not well organised within Bosnia and Herzegovina, although of course there were some people who originated from Serbia proper involved in the armed forces of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But how would you characterise the conflict? I know that you characterise it as internal, but between what groups?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I would say between the VRS and the central government forces, but the VRS supported by ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: VRS being the insurgent force ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the rebellious forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: --- and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the other side?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, there still is a problem. That would be our position if the central government of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be in control. I just told you that they claimed that Bosnia and Herzegovina was a state. I told you about the precipitous recognition of that. If one thinks that the Bosnian Serbs, the inhabitants of the Republika Srpska, the Serbian Republic, were not in whatever way under their control, you could even ask yourself which was the state at that time, but the Appeals Chamber has given a clear decision that the Republika Srpska cannot be regarded as a state, so, therefore, not for constitutional reasons, I have to regard the Republika Srpska as the rebellious forces against the central government forces. That was my conclusion, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, did Dr. Gow testify at the very end of his testimony that the JNA was present in Bosnia and Herzegovina? When I say the JNA, I mean the JNA of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. He mentioned several incidents right at the end of his testimony in the eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you recall that? I have not read it since, so maybe I am wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly, your Honour. I know that also Mr. Doko has stated that there had been some problems in totally different places.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Not Mr. Doko, this was Dr. Gow. We will check it again. Of course, I suppose, as you say, this would mean that we would then apply Article 3 or Common Article 3 to these alleged offences if we found Mr. Tadic guilty as opposed to Article 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was speaking about whether Article 2 could be applied in an internal conflict, at least a part that could apply under Article 3 or Article 5 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, it is really academic in so far as the ultimate outcome because there is overlap between Article 3 and Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It is just as academic as charging the defendant with all three categories of crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Orie. Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honours, I will only deal with a few legal matters that have not been addressed before. Consequently, I will only add little to our position as described in the pretrial brief with regard to more substantial evidence. The first observation deals with deportation as this allegation especially mentioned in the description of the various acts of paragraph 4 of the indictment. The acts of this paragraph are in the present indictment charged under count 1 as a crime against humanity. Originally, however -- I refer the Court to the draft as attached to the Prosecution motion seeking for a leave to amend the indictment of 31st July last year -- paragraph 4 had two headings, "persecution" and "deportation", and all acts of paragraph 4 were charged with three counts; one count of persecution and two counts of deportation. Deportation was originally specifically charged as a crime against humanity under Article 5(d) of the Statute and as a grave breach of the Geneva Convention under Article 2(g) of the Statute. When your Chamber ruled that the act contained in paragraph 4 of the draft indictment should be cleared more in detail, the Prosecution dropped these two counts on deportation and changed the heading of this paragraph into persecution only. Whereas the present paragraph 4 under the heading of persecution only mounts up to a charge of persecution under Article 5(h) of the Statute, one might wonder whether this charge also encompasses deportation. Our position is it is not. Why not? Well, because of the system of Article 5 of the Statute. We believe that it is significant that the crime of deportation is listed as a crime against humanity under Article 5(d), separate from persecution of section (h) of this Article. The persecution would encompass deportation, why then to enumerate this crime separately under different headings? We have found no authority arguing the contrary, and I note that the Prosecution did not argue that deportation is a part of persecution, nor in their pretrial brief, neither in their closing argument this week. We, therefore, submit to the Court that deportation is a separate crime from persecution and, consequently, that parts of paragraph 4 that mount up to deportation, if proven, cannot be qualified as persecution. If the Court may find so, another question may arise, whereas the Prosecution argued in a pretrial brief that the court in that case may have the authority to render findings of guilt for offences other than those specifically charged; in our pretrial brief we have denied such authority on two grounds: First, we have submitted that such findings would violate the principle of legality as recognised in international law and, moreover, because we believe that such alternative findings have no basis in international law. It is not a part of customary international law. Let me elaborate that a little. International law recognises that it is a basic requirement of the criminal law that a defendant should be made aware of every single element that constitutes the offence. Civil law jurisdictions deal with this requirement by statutory law only, while common law jurisdictions nowadays show a mixed practice. Codification of substantive criminal law was in common law practice not always required to accept common law offences as a basis for conviction. This practice did not raise serious problems of awareness because in those jurisdictions there has always been a long standing tradition and history upon which the defendant and counsel could rely. But this practice has changed. I suggest that in most common law jurisdictions substantive law is increasingly regulated by statutory law. New crimes are, as a rule, penalised through statutory law. So we believe that it is a fair statement to say that the all over trend in this respect is that civil and common law grow towards another if it comes to a new law. I have little problem to submit to you that the international humanitarian law is new, is a new and not yet fully known branch of tree called the criminal law. The world community has created these new crimes that only have a brief tradition which were, unfortunately, almost forgotten again after the closure of the post World War II trials in Nuremberg and Tokyo. Since then, only a few specialists were aware of this area of international law. Most practising lawyers had little or no knowledge of the variety of crimes under the Conventions and the scope of these crimes. Indeed, defining international customary law is difficult and gives rise to disputes about scope or specific topics. Being aware of this, the legislators of the Statute confined themselves to jurisdictional methods instead of specifying the violations of International Humanitarian Law. The Statute of the Tribunal does not encompass a code of offences, but relies upon offences under customary law that only incidentally have been developed by international tribunals and with rare application under domestic law. Consequently, and different to the practice in domestic common law jurisdictions, there are hardly any case law in history upon which the defendant and counsel can rely in addressing an indictment under the international jurisdiction of this Tribunal. Under these circumstances, the lack of statutory provisions may give rise to violations of the principle of legality when it is without good cause assumed that the defendant is aware of every single element that constitutes the offence. It is in this context that I recall that the trial against Dusko Tadic started with an exchange of pretrial briefs where both parties were uncertain about the scope of the indicted offence. Under these circumstances, it seems not fair to ambush a defendant with findings of guilt of violations of unchartered humanitarian law that were not indicted. Consequently, we submit to the Court that any finding of guilt must be limited to offences as charged only. Let us just for the sake of the argument suppose that the Court has the authority to render findings of guilt for offences other than those specifically charged. In that case, questions may arise about the scope of the deportation as a crime under Article 2(g) of the Statute. The pretrial briefs of the Prosecution and the Defence demonstrate the difference in opinion whether deportation should be defined in accordance with Article 49 of the Geneva Convention, or that rather definition of Article 85(4)(a) may also be taken into consideration. Then, in the narrow definition of Article 49, unlawful deportation is limited to transfers from occupied territory to the territory of the occupying power (or any foreign territory). Under Article 85, though, the Protocol 1, deportation within the occupied territory would also fall within the definition. Even if an armed conflict of international character would have existed (which, as Mr. Orie set out, we deny), we suggest that the Prosecution has not presented evidence that would prove the existence of an occupation on behalf of the Belgrade government, being in occupation, a takeover by a foreign occupying power as a de facto administrator. This also implicates that neither under the wide nor under the narrow definition unlawful deportation took place, being there no occupied territory. Under the narrow definition we suggest that no evidence has been presented that would prove the deportation of persons in the territory of the occupying power. The narrow definition is, in our submission, the only one that would be applicable (if at all, since there is no specific deportation charge). With regard to the wider definition, I note that the customary status of Protocol 1 is too uncertain to accept it as acceptable customary law. In sum, your Honours, we believe that there is no sufficient legal room for an alternative finding of guilt of deportation under Article 2(g) of the Statute. Another matter that almost follows from the same argument deriving from the principle of legality is the number of your findings of guilt within a specific count. We suggest that proof of more than one act may only lead to a finding of guilt of one and not of multiple crimes. If we focus, for example, on paragraph 4, the indictment clearly charges that Dusko Tadic by his participation in the acts described in the factual array, committed a crime -- I emphasise a crime -- as described in count 1, and not a plurality of crimes under Article 5(h) of the Statute. Of course, the same applies for the other charges. We, therefore, submit to the Court that the accused can only be found guilty for each count once leaving the weight of multiple acts, though, as a matter for sentencing. As regards to torture ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can you tell me, if you look at paragraph 6, for instance -- I could take any paragraph other than paragraph 4, but paragraph 6 is the first available one -- do you say that there can only be six, seven offences, in other words, under count 5 only one crime and conviction?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What I am saying, your Honour, is that, for example, count 5 may lead to a breach and not to breaches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, but it can lead to one, then count 6 can also lead to a separate one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have discussed that in the context of the form of the indictment. I have taken very good notice of your decision on that matter. That is the reason why I am not discussing that matter again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. That is clear then.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is not exactly clear to me. When you say a grave breach, are you saying that since there are multiple victims that it should be treated as one transaction and Mr. Tadic could not be found guilty of a grave breach for each victim?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is what I am saying, your Honour -- if proven, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand. It is all hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: All under that heading. As regards to torture, your Honours, as charged under count 8 of paragraph 6, I only have a brief remark to make for as far as the Prosecution dealt with that matter. I stress that, in our opinion, an expansion of the purpose behind the infliction of pain to the extent that any reason based on discrimination of any kind would be included has not yet reached the status of international customary law. The Prosecution has not shown that it does. The third topic I want to touch on is the inhumane act as charged under count 20 of paragraph 9. We disagree with the Prosecution when they argue that the indicted act, if proven to be an infliction on a dead body, may establish a crime against humanity. We believe that there is no basis in international customary law for such novelty interpretation. The Prosecution has not shown any authority for their position. We suggest, your Honours, that the significant character of crimes against humanity is that only human life is protected under Article 5 of the Statute, not dead bodies. We believe that actions directed against dead bodies cannot be seen as actions directed against civilian people as enumerated under Article 5 of the Statute, simply because it is hard to believe that one can murder, one can exterminate, one can enslave, deport, imprison or persecute for discriminating reasons a dead body, if we simply follow the wording of Article 5. May I now briefly turn ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, I do not want to interrupt you, but I have to; what about an offence against human dignity? I understand that if a person is dead you cannot kill them, that makes sense. But would it be an offence against a person's dignity, whether they are dead or alive, to treat a person in that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You are referring to Article 5, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: "The International Tribunal shall have the power to prosecute persons responsible for the following crimes when committed in armed conflict, whether international or internal in character, and directed against any civilian population: murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation, imprisonment, torture, rape, persecutions on political, racial and religious grounds or inhumane acts". I did not quite understand your question, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Never mind. I will withdraw it. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I now briefly turn to the composition of the indictment, since the factual descriptions of paragraph 4 encompasses some repetition. This repetition is in the first place that Dusko Tadic is charged with the seizure and transfer of non-Serbs to the camps of Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje as described in a portion of subparagraph 4.1 as well as in the remaining portion of 4.3 and as a separate allegation of subparagraph 4.4. The differences in wording of these subparagraphs, as far as they deal with seizure and transport of non-Serbs in camps, seems not relevant; whereas all these subparagraphs result in only one count, persecution on political, racial and/or religious grounds, a crime against humanity under Article 5(h) of the Statute. If we focus on the time frames of these portions, it appears that a period of time of each subparagraph under which the alleged acts may have taken place overlap the period of time of the other subparagraphs. This overlap implicates that the seizure, selection and transportation of non-Serbs for detention in all the camps between 25th May and 31st December 1992 of subparagraph 4.4 totally absorbs the seizure and transfer of non-Serbs from the Kozarac area to Trnopolje camp between 25th May and 31st December 1992, subparagraph 4.3. The same applies to subparagraph 4.1 if we realise that the Court did not receive any evidence about the seizure and transfer of non-Serbs from Kozarac and the surrounding area to detention centres on 24th May 1992. As the relevant time of subparagraph 4.1 is effectively limited to the time between 25th and 27th May 1992, also this portion of subparagraph 4.1 is totally absorbed by subparagraph 4.4. Whereas the general part in paragraph 4 limits the non-Serbs to residence of opstina Prijedor and the camps to Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje, the indicated parts of 4.1 and 4.3 are materially encompassed by the allegation of subparagraph 4.4 between 25th May and 31st December 1992. A similar issue is the repeated reference in paragraph 4 to other charges of the indictment. Subparagraph 4.1 refers to the charge of paragraph 12, apparently with the purpose to have the alleged acts of charge 12 to mount up to the count of persecution. However, a reference to an act that allegedly happened about 14th June 1992 cannot fit in the time frame of 24th to 27th May 1992, as described in subparagraph 4.1. It needs little explanation that the reference in paragraph 4.2 to the withdrawn charge of paragraph 5 is totally useless since this charge has been withdrawn. If I may now turn briefly to the criminal responsibility, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Which paragraph? Which charge has been withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The charge at paragraph 5, though the reference in 4.2 is still there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me ask you though one question, Mr. Wladimiroff. Regarding paragraph 11, speaking hypothetically, that in the substantive counts, counts 24 to 28, charges offences on May 27th 1992. Could that constitute, that transaction constitute, a violation of the legal bases cited in counts 24 to 28 and also constitute persecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Not in the context of this indictment, your Honour, because -- well, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is 11 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I thought you were referring to 12.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, but 11 you do not have a problem; 12 you have a problem because it is clearly outside of the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have tried to explain that whether it could constitute a persecution or not, well, as a matter of fact, where there is a reference in 4 to paragraph 11, one could argue that it is indicted because it is a part of the factual -- it is indicted as a persecution because the factual array of 11 is incorporated in 4.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So it is indicted as persecution because it is also indicted as a grave breach violation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, and I have not opposed that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You have not what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have not opposed that because it is a part of the factual array and we were aware that 11 was also a basis for the charge of persecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Does that mean that you think that it would be proper, assuming the necessary finding of fact, to convict on one of these later paragraphs, the counts under them, and also the count under persecution, although the same facts are relied on in both?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We have two issues here, your Honour, as I see it. The factual array of paragraph 11 is incorporated in paragraph 4. Therefore, those facts of paragraph 11 may mount up to count 1, if proven. Another issue is whether the facts of paragraph 11 may mount up to counts 24 up to 28. That issue, as I already said, has been dealt with by your Court while we were discussing the form of the indictment. So I have not discussed that matter again. It is res judicata.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: And it will be dealt with on sentence, in effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, let me now turn to criminal responsibility, if I may. Article 7.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you turn to that, let me ask you one question on the elements. In your pretrial brief regarding the charges for persecution on political, racial or religious grounds, you were concerned with the lack of definition of the specified acts. Would you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The lack of clarity is still a matter to be decided by the Court, whether that is sufficiently established in customary humanitarian law to accept the standard that will fit for the facts as indicted. So we have left it there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you are saying that there are certain acts that have not been made criminal under customary international law?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I can accept that proposition, but I thought that you were concerned with the lack of specificity or definition in the indictment. But, if that is not your position, then it is just a question of law, whether or not these acts have been made criminal and individual responsibility under customary and international law. I do not want to take too much time. If that is your position, that is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think I will deal with that later, if I may, because then I have to look at the pretrial brief again, how that fits after the receiving of the evidence. So I will come back to that, your Honour, if I may? Are there any other questions?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Article 7 of the Statute places criminal responsibility on those who planned, instigated, ordered or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation or execution of violations in a context which I will shortly deal with. Reading the indictment, I notice that the wording of the charges does not follow the specific wording of Article 7. Charge 4 for example, charges the defendant, on the one hand, with "physical participation" or "participation" in acts or "physical involvement" or "active involvement" in acts, or "taking part" in acts and "being included in Serb forces" who committed acts and, on the other hand, it charges Dusko Tadic with the commission of crimes because of his participation in these acts. So we have this word "participation" in two different contexts here. The factual descriptions, such as "participation", "involvement", "taking part" or "being included" are practically synonymous to each other, so I will confine myself to the word "participation" instead of repeating during my arguments all these variations. If you look at the charges of 6 up to 12, they accuse the defendant with being "included in a group of Serb forces" or "armed Serbs" that committed crimes (which I will further call "participation" again). Further, he is charged with the commission of crimes because of his participation in these acts. It seems to me that the word "participation" is used in the charges in two different ways. First, participation as a factual type of involvement or otherwise taking part in crimes and, second, as a qualification of the legal type of involvement, claiming that participation is the commission of the crimes as listed in the counts. That is the phrasing in the indictment. Whereas the factual description of any behaviour as participation cannot be severed from the legal meaning of that behaviour in the context of criminal responsibility, it makes sense to analyse the types of responsibility under the Statute first. Participation in the context of the Statute is, contrary to the assertions of the Prosecution, not an almost unrestricted notion. It is way beyond its limits to say that all those who contribute -- I quote the Prosecution -- "in any manner whatsoever" or -- I quote again -- "regardless of their specific roles to the commission of a violation are guilty". From paragraph 54 of the Report of the Secretary-General of May 3rd 1993, it appears that "participation" is clearly restricted to planning, instigating ordering, committing or otherwise aiding and abetting in the planning, and there follows the whole sentence as we can see it in Article 7.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is it paragraph 44, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: 54, your Honour. Having read the report of the International Law Commission of 6th May to 27th July 1996, where these concepts of planning, instigating, ordering, committing or otherwise aiding and abetting are further elaborated, the Defence does not argue with the criminal responsibility of those who planned, instigated or ordered the crimes. These notions seem to be clear but not relevant in this case. Participation, though, does not in itself establish that the participant has committed a crime under Article 7(1) of the Statute. Participation may only be qualified as the commission of a crime when the perpetrator meets all the elements that establish the crime. We submit that physical participation or participation, or physical involvement or active involvement, or taking part, or being included in Serb forces who committed crimes as described in charge 4, for example, does in itself not establish the commission of a crime under Article 7. We also submit that being included in a group of Serb forces or armed Serbs that committed crimes, as described in the other charges, neither in itself establishes the commission of a crime under Article 7. It is clear that the factual description of participation in the crimes charged in the indictment refers to being an accessory to and not being the perpetrator of a crime. Accessories, according to Article 7 of the Statute, are those who aided and abetted in planning, preparation or execution of violations of International Humanitarian Law.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Wladimiroff, are you saying then that the word "committed" in Article 7(1) requires physical, actual participation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour. That is not what I am saying. What I am saying is that the commission of a crime is only there when the perpetrator meets all the elements that establish the crime.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: He by himself.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- does that beg the question of whether or not he can meet all of those elements if he participates in the execution of it in a way that does not include his actual physical participation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour, because in that case we would argue that he is an accessory to the crime.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you saying that accessory then would fit within the individual criminal responsibility as defined under the Statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am going to deal with that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is it "yes" or "no"? Then you can deal with it, but just give me an answer if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: An accessory is covered by aiding and abetting.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What it means, though, is a different question. But I am making a difference here, if I make myself clear, between the use of the word "participation" referring to a perpetrator, which can only be the case if the one who participated has met all the elements of the crime, and the participator, who is only an aider and an abettor. That is what I am firstly saying here. During the hearing of the motion on dismissal, the Defence, as I may remember, took the position that participation as aiding and abetting within the criminal responsibility of the statute requires active involvement in the execution of a crime, and that it would not be enough to be present whilst a crime is committed if one does not take part in it or does not act in concert with those who commit it. That is a statement I want to elaborate on a little. As is the case in all jurisdictions known to the Defence, the International Law Commission has emphasised that an accomplice is only aiding and abetting if he knowingly provides assistance to the perpetrator, report pages 18, 24 to 25. Accordingly, we submit that furthering or facilitating a crime committed by someone else is not punishable if one does not realise that the other commits or will commit a crime, or if the act done was not a likely consequence of the offence in which the accused participated. The underlining principle here is that only criminal intent materialised by behaviour is punishable. This is also recognised in the aftermath of Nuremberg. I refer to the Justice Trial and the trial against Oswald and others, as cited by the Prosecution in their submission of November 20th. What are the requirements then? The first requirement for participation in the meaning of aiding and abetting of violations of International Humanitarian Law under the Statute is, therefore, proof of knowingly assisting in the commission of a crime. Consistent to domestic jurisdictions, the International Law Commission also emphasised that an accomplice must provide the kind of assistance which contributes directly and substantially to the commission of the crime. The assistance must at the very least have facilitated the commission of the crime in a significant way. Contrary to the argument of the Prosecution, the Defence believes that the Mauthausen case does not set a different standard here. The engagement of the defendants in the Mauthausen case, described in the decision as being engaged, I quote now, "in any manner whatsoever" does not implicate that any assistance can qualify as aiding and abetting. The crux of the opinion in the Mauthausen case was that all defendants were engaged in the operation of the concentration camp. That specific engagement was as such proof of a direct and substantial contribution to the crimes committed there. So the second requirement seems to be participation in the meaning of aiding and abetting, that there should be proof of a direct and substantial furtherance of the commission of the crime. The references to national jurisdictions given by the Prosecution do not, as a source of customary law, when those cases did not deal with violations of International Humanitarian Law in a domestic setting, bring us much further. It only shows that aiding and abetting lead to a variety of case law and that a participant may be convicted as an accessory. But it is not directly relevant for our case as long as those cases were not dealt with in the context of a violation of International Humanitarian Law, though in a domestic setting.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Wladimiroff, what do you mean by "substantial furtherance"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will elaborate that later on, your Honour. So I hope to answer your question then.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Maybe I should just listen, but can you just give me a little clue now since I have a question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I rather prefer to develop the argument in which it will be dealt with instead of picking out a part of it and giving it to you at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think in that response you are very fortunate that you are not in a national jurisdiction, but go ahead. Read your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We find it somewhat strange, your Honour, that in the context of the post World War II -- no, I am reading it wrongly. We find it somewhat strange that in the context of International Humanitarian Law the Prosecution refers to cases of the German Reichsgericht of the German Empire of the last century and of the German Reichsgericht of the Weimar Republic and, moreover, to decisions of the Reichsgericht of Germans of Hitler's Germany. This last reference is, therefore, indeed quite peculiar because it is dealt with in the context of International Humanitarian Law. I may recall that the judges of Nazi Germany were tried in the Justice trial. Anyhow, whereas witnesses in the Tadic case claim they have seen Dusko Tadic near or at the scene of the crime, an important issue in this case is the question whether such presence, if proved, can lead to a criminal responsibility. I have two observations here. First, physical participation requires an active commitment as described before, and excludes being present without acting in concert with those who committed the crimes. Second, proof of a sighting by witnesses of the accused near the scene of a crime without any further proof of involvement does not, in our opinion, establish a criminal responsibility under Article 7 of the Statute. Proof of a sighting of the accused at the scene of a crime or whilst a crime is committed is, as we already said during the hearing of the defence motion on dismissal, as such not enough under Article 7, if one is not proved to have taken part in the crime or does not act in concert with those who commit it. We deny that the most marginal act of assistance or encouragement would, as seems to be the case in Australian law, in cases where they did not deal with International Humanitarian Law, amount to an act of complicity in the crime, because this is, as we submit to the Court, not well established customary international law. Here we make a distinction between culpability under an international jurisdiction for violations of International Humanitarian Law and common crimes tried in a national jurisdiction. If presence is punishable in a national jurisdiction, it usually concerns participation with a group of persons who committed the common crimes. The actions of such groups are often directed by internal dynamics within the group, such as macho behaviour, leading to criminal acts. Timely breaking up with the group is not dependent on external factors, but only on the ability to free oneself of these internal dynamics. Cases of violations of International Humanitarian Law usually concern persons acting under abnormal circumstances, such as war. In these cases, not only considerations of an internal nature are relevant, but also external factors, such as totalitarian local regime that may have a much larger effect on the actor. Evidence in this case shows that in 1992 people in the opstina Prijedor were living in chaotic times fearing all kinds of risks of their life, health, work and home under the violent and arbitrary rule of the local Crisis Staff. That did not only affect the Muslims, but it also affected the Serbs. We have heard evidence in this case about Serbs who were also confined in camps. We have heard evidence of Serbs who were driven out of the country. So a lot of people, also Serbs, were at risk of being confronted with violations of humanitarian law or were being present when these violations were committed. It is clear that the context of the commission of common crimes is different to the context of the commission of war crimes or crimes against humanity. In the context of a common crime culpable presence may be reasoned by the possibility of the accused to disassociate himself from the crime. But, given the difference in context, we take the position that the presence whilst crimes under your jurisdiction are committed should not automatically be judged in line with the case law of criminal responsibility for common crimes under national jurisdictions. The citing of the Mauthausen case by the Prosecution in this context of culpable presence is misplaced, since the decision in that case does not establish that the mere presence will be enough to establish criminal responsibility under the Statute. We agree with the Prosecution where they argue that the mere presence, without proof of other factors, does not give rise to criminal liability. We suggest that the presence should at least be proven to be significant to the commission of the crime, and that the proof of the significance of presence should not be speculative but material. The presence of an accused can only further the commission of a crime when there is a significant causal relation between the commission of the crime and the accused's presence. In other words, the presence must be significant, either because of a prior agreement between the accused and the perpetrator, or perpetrators, or because of the influence of the accused's presence at the commission of the crime; for example, the encouragement given by the presence of the accused to the commission of the crime. We, therefore, agree with the passages of the Coney case cited by the Prosecution reading: "The fact that a person was voluntarily and purposely present witnessing the commission of a crime and offered no opposition though he might reasonably be expected to prevent it and had the power to do so, or at least express his dissent, might in some circumstances afford cogent evidence upon which a jury would be justified in finding that he wilfully encouraged and so aided and abetted". Indeed, under abnormal circumstances such as we are dealing with, bystanders cannot be held culpable if they are silently present. If this were the case, most residents of opstina Prijedor would be culpable because of their presence whilst atrocities are committed in that area. These specific circumstances explain why we cannot have it the American way, where US courts apparently expect a bystander to voice some opposition or surprise if he were not a party to the crime. I refer to the State v. Parker case. In the Tadic case, we hold that the mere presence at the scene, even having knowledge or reasons to believe, as everyone may have had in those days, that a crime is to be committed, is not in itself sufficient to establish aiding and abetting under the Statute, because the conduct must be in furtherance of the conflict. If there is only a passive presence, how is that in furtherance? The Defence has not found cases where visitors to Nazi camps were sentenced because of their presence in those camps without proof of any further involvement. The relevant factor in post World War II cases cited by the Prosecution was the involvement with the running of the camp, not the presence as such. It was the running of the camp and being present there. As far as presence was relevant, it appeared to be interpreted as an encouragement because the accused was one of those who was involved in the operation of the camp. Such presence could, indeed, and we agree, be significant. Consequently, we suggest that a visit to the camp does not as such imply criminal responsibility, not being involved with the operation of the camp. We also suggest that presence in a camp is not in itself an encouragement to commit crimes. Even repetitive presence does not alter this position, since each presence, as we hold, should be judged on its own merits,. If not, just as an example, English or continental Judges, for example, would accept that regular visitors of football stadiums, where, as we all know, a lot of violence is committed by visitors, would establish a criminal responsibility. The position of the Prosecution on this matter would mean that having been seen several times doing nothing indicates that you deliberately participated in the wrong doing. We cannot accept that kind of collective responsibility. I refer to page 6500, lines 22 up to 25. For culpable presence, it will be necessary to prove that the visitor acted in such a way that his presence was knowingly a relevant factor to further the commission of a crime. At this point, I may draw the attention of the Court to the French text of Article 7 reading "aide et encourage". I emphasise "encourage", which word may sound familiar to you. The Prosecution has also raised the argument of the Dachau case, that acting in a common plan to commit the indicted crimes establishes criminal responsibility under the Statute, so they say. The fundamental problem of the Dachau judgment, however, is the requirement that the accused by his conduct must encourage, aid and abet or participate in enforcing the system. We encounter here the same words, participation, aiding and abetting and encouragement. I already discussed that. The reference by the Prosecution to the Mauthausen case in this context does not bring us much further, as again all the defendants in that case were in some way in control or stationed at or engaged in the operation of the Mauthausen camp. Dusko Tadic is not accused of being in control or stationed at or engaged in the operation of Omarska, Keraterm or Trnopolje. The same applies for the reference to the Belsen case. The Almelo trial, as cited by the Prosecution, might have defined a simple collective responsibility. However, the bottom line in that case still is that an accused is only guilty if he was present at the same time as the perpetrators, taking part in a common enterprise. Collective action is more than simply being present, and the Defence has, therefore, no problem with this reference. Criminal responsibility: we have no problem with this reference, your Honour, as long as criminal responsibility deriving from acting in a common plan to commit crimes emerged from a common criminal intent to commit a crime. We accept that this common intent implies that an accused is also culpable for crimes that would be a likely consequence of carrying out the common intent. But we strongly oppose, however, the idea (which seems to be a part of Canadian law) that someone can be held responsible for the consequences of a common plan he ought to have known, whether he, in fact, knew of it or not. According to a basic principle in criminal law, most criminal laws held that someone is only responsible if he or she is personally culpable because of intent or actual knowledge. We strongly oppose the idea that someone can be held responsible for the consequences of a common plan he ought to have known. It seems just to limit the culpability for a common plan to plans of criminal activity which are actually known to the accused. Responsibility is, therefore, only proved, we submit to you, if there is sufficient proof of the common plan and the accused's knowledge of it, or intent to have the plan (and its foreseeable consequences) executed. This proof may be derived from the behaviour of the accused and of those with whom he allegedly collaborated. Again, we submit that this proof should not be speculative, for example, by the fact that the accused could be associated with others of similar political ideas, but material. Look to his behaviour. Evidence received by your Court indicates that Tadic was not a well-informed participant of actions undertaken by the military. On the contrary, we have heard sufficient evidence of Dusko Tadic avoiding to be involved with the army. With regard to the actions of others than military, in the eyes of the Prosecution as they said yesterday, everything the accused did paralleled what everyone else was doing. This position, your Honours, if proven, would indicate that the alleged actions of Tadic were not a part of a plan, not a knowingly involvement in an agreed plan, but on the contrary individual actions without an agreed basis. It certainly needs a higher level of commitment to accept that someone acted in connection with others or in concert with others to carry out a common intent. Although it is not established that a domestic topic is a part of customary international law, I might assist the Court in explaining the Dutch law as cited by the Prosecution in their submission on Article 7. Participating in a criminal organisation, that is, a group of two or more persons that have set out to commit crimes, establishes only responsibility for any act committed by any other member of this group if two requirements are met in Dutch law. First, the group of two or more persons that has set out to commit crimes should not be an incidental one, but a structured cooperation. Second, the accused should have participated in the structured co-operation by supporting acts that may further, or are related to, the realisation of the purpose to commit crimes. If I may return to the law of this Tribunal, we do not believe that the scope of Article 7(1) is so broad that the Prosecution would not have to show that the accused acted in connection with others, that he had an agreement. On the contrary, we believe that the Prosecution has the burden of proof of these elements of these requirements of individual criminal responsibility under the Statute. These are the limits, your Honours, of criminal responsibility. To deduce from the presence, if proved, of the accused at the scene of a crime that he participated in the crime would, in our submission, be totally wrong. Your Honours, we have come to the end of our arguments and when I had prepared the closing argument I intended to wind up all portions of our submissions as presented to you by each of us. For the sake of time, however, I will not summarise the observations we have been making on behalf of the Defence. I am convinced, your Honours, that this Court has concerned itself with all the details of the case and your questions have been very encouraging for us to put forward our case. So I have decided to confine myself to a formal conclusion rather than a material one. Our final submission to you is that the evidence presented by the Prosecution witnesses to you leads inevitably to the conclusion that the Prosecution has not met its burden of proof as required. The evidence fails for the reasons as set out to you in detail and, moreover, because of the convincing evidence with regard to the alibi of the accused, which evidence has aroused substantial and reasonable doubt. We trust that you will give full weight to the legal argument raised by the Defence and, in sum, we strongly believe you will not find Dusko Tadic guilty as charged. Let me close, your Honours, with Abraham Lincoln's letter of 6th October 1883 to Charles Drake and others on civil wars and what happens in them. I quote: "Actual war coming, blood grows hot, and blood is spilt. Thought is forced from old channels into confusion. Deception breeds and thrives. Confidence dies, and universal suspicion reigns. Each man feels an impulse to kill his neighbour, lest he be first killed by him. Revenge and retaliation follow. And all this ... may be among honest men only. But this is not all. Every foul bird comes abroad, and every dirty reptile rises up. These add crime to confusion. Strong measures, deemed indispensable but harsh at best, such men make worse by mal-administration. Murders for old grudges, and murders for gain, proceed under any cloak that will best cover for the occasion. These causes amply account for what has happened in Missourie" or, may I add, in Bosnia. This has happened all over the world when local conflicts turn into civil war. Indeed, civil wars are not only about armed conflicts but also about retaliation and false allegations. These ingredients are a perfect recipe for a miscarriage of justice when prejudiced witnesses. Who fit second hand accounts into their own accounts, can proceed under the cloak of a victim. It would be a tragedy, your Honours, if this were to happen in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. 10.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, would you like to begin the Prosecution rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. In fact, your Honour, Mr. Keegan will begin the Prosecution rebuttal with a very short discussion of some points concerning issues of international armed conflict. Then Mr. Tieger will speak to you about evidence concerning the character of the accused, inconsistency in his testimony and prior statements and also between his and other witnesses. Then I will speak with you very briefly about some of the factual issues raised by the Defence and some additional points of law. So at this time I would ask Mr. Keegan to come forward.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I would like to first address a point raised by Judge Stephen with respect to the attack on Hambarine. That attack did, in fact, come after the date of the technical withdrawal of the JNA which was, as publicly pronounced, 19th May, and the attack on Hambarine, of course, not beginning until 23rd May. But, of course, we would then reference you to the facts which indicate that the JNA did not withdraw, including Prosecution Exhibit 60, the United Nations resolution imposing sanctions on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in part for its stay to withdraw its forces from Bosnia-Herzegovina. That resolution was dated 30th May 1992. What I wanted to talk about briefly was the meaning and language of the Nicaragua case, since there have been questions about whether the requirement is to be an agent or organ, and then briefly the citizenship issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The date of the takeover of Prijedor was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Of Prijedor was 30th April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Well before, in other words, a withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The fact that it was bloodless does not necessarily stop it being a hostile act?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, in fact, the text of Nicaragua and the other decisions or documents we referenced talk about armed force, not that there has to be actual combat in the sense of blood being shed. With respect to Nicaragua, the language actually used is "the acts of other groups that amount to or can be categorised as such to equate them as an organ or acting on behalf of the other entity", the other State. So that is where that language comes from, Nicaragua. The word "agent" is used in the Appeals Chamber decision and by the Prosecution as a shorthand for the term "acting on behalf of". So that is where the word "agent" comes from. But that is the actual standard found in paragraphs 109 and 115 in the Nicaragua decision. It is the acts of the groups, such they can be considered as an organ of or acting on behalf of the other state. With respect to the issue of the evidence of international armed conflict, first, I would note that in citing some of the Prosecution evidence Mr. Orie curiously neglected to mention Prosecution Exhibit 180, the notice published by the second army of the Yugoslav Army in the Serbian State paper indicating its continuing involvement in the armed conflict in the Trebinje region of Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout the summer and fall of 1992, in addition to the conclusions raised by Mr. Vulliamy in which he was linking the similarity of what he saw in Vlasenica to the observations he made in Croatia and the JNA operation there. With respect to this absurd outcome argument raised first in the appeal brief, we would note that, in fact, since it is recognised in international law that a conflict can be rendered international by the acts of other groups, irregulars or mercenaries acting on behalf of a state, it is clear then that the acts committed by those groups render the victims of those protected persons in the context of an international armed conflict. When you put that in the context of armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina in particular, it is an interesting dilemma that the Appeals Chamber has produced by the nature of its decision on this issue, because in fact it declares a conflict in Bosnia prior to May 19th as an international armed conflict. At that time there is no doubt that units of the JNA included Bosnian-Serb soldiers and included paramilitary units and police forces acting at the direction of the JNA committing acts against Bosnian Muslims. Apparently, there is no question that at that time the Bosnian-Muslim victims would be protected persons in respect of those acts committed by Bosnian-Serb persons against them at the direction of JNA. The dilemma there is what status are the Bosnian-Serb civilians who would have then been subject to acts, perhaps, in combat or in reprisal? One must assume that the Appeals Chamber would find that they would have been protected persons as well at that point. If that is, in fact, the case, post May 19th where the facts clearly indicate that this redesignation, public redesignation, of the JNA into the VRS and the Yugoslav Army, that that part of the army designated as the VRS continued to act in accordance with the plans and strategy initiated by the JNA, that their acts continued to be committed against Bosnian Muslim and Croat civilians, and if, in fact, the determination is reached that that continued to be an international armed conflict, it is our submission the Bosnian-Serb civilians who may have been victims during that time (and the evidence as to that has not been presented in this case, so this is purely a legal issue) that they too would have continued in their status as protected persons. There is the issue that arises in citizenship. It is a recognised doctrine that in cases of state succession (which we have here) that there is the right of a presumption of citizenship in the new entity so that no one is deprived of the protection of citizenship of a state, but there is also the right of election, which we note in our response to the Defence reply on the Prosecution pretrial brief which we submitted on April 26th. There is a discussion in there on this issue. It is that right of election and the other issues regarding citizenship which the Appeals Chamber, frankly, ignored in its decision on this issue. Where we find support for the fact that based on the facts you have the declaration in January of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, promulgated in February '92 (not December, as mentioned by Mr. Orie), where they declare themselves citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as well as the public statements that followed thereafter where the elected officials clearly indicated the intent was to establish Serbian citizenship not only in the entity but also in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We believe that those statements give an indication of how those people considered the status of their citizenship. So it is from those documents and with the recognised issues of the law that exist that we find support for the fact that you can find an international armed conflict and that persons on both sides were protected persons. I would note just the one final issue, because Nicaragua was addressed so much, and that is, in fact, that in paragraph 219 of that decision the Court found that the conflict between the Contras and the Nicaraguan armed forces was an internal nature, despite the support of the United States. But we find here that the facts are substantially different which we have noted in our brief and I will not cover again. Finally, just on a related point on the issue of plunder: of course, "plunder" is the term used in Article 3(e) of our Statute, which is why it was used by the Prosecution in its submissions and in the indictment. "Pillage" is, in fact, a term used in the Geneva Conventions and in The Hague Conventions and Regulations from which our Statute is drawn, but you will find both in, for example, Blacks law dictionary, the dictionary of the international law of armed conflict of the ICRC and in military law, in fact, the military Judges bench book for the United States, that "pillage" and "plunder" are synonymous terms. The basic definition is to unlawfully seize or appropriate public or private property by force or means of violence; so, in effect, fact robbery, if you will, as mentioned by Mr. Kay. I would note just for the Court that we believe the reading of the Defence of the term of the language of the indictment is incorrect. In that paragraph where we speak of "plunder", it is alleged that the accused and others destroyed and plundered homes and other property. We were using the word "plunder" in the traditional sense, meaning they went in and took property as well as destroyed the homes, not that they actually took the homes, so, just to clarify that point. Now I would invite any questions the Court may have on these issues?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have no questions, thank you, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to identification procedures the Defence first raises the theoretical concern raised by Dr. Wagenaar about the photo line up which he otherwise approved, and that was that he did not know where the foils where from. Mr. Wladimiroff suggests this is somehow still an issue, despite the fact that nine of the 12 foils turned out to be from former Yugoslavia. Now Mr. Wladimiroff complains that we do not know exactly where in former Yugoslavia they are from, and this is completely irrelevant. Just very quickly to remind the Court, this issue arose when the doctor theorized that, perhaps, subjects from former Yugoslavia would be able to distinguish among the ethnic groups. He then later conducted an experiment in Belgrade to test that. As he said, "I was quite reassured after seeing those results that nothing has gone grossly wrong in the selection of the foils". Nevertheless, he had still had some lingering concern that perhaps none of the people he had shown, none of those foils, had been from former Yugoslavia and, therefore, the experiment which asked people to categorise the people, the foils, as Macedonians, Croats, Slovenians and so on might not have been possible. He did say, however, that this concern would be entirely alleviated if he found that eight or nine of the photographs of the foils were persons from former Yugoslavia. That is what he was discussing throughout his entire discussion of that issue, persons from former Yugoslavia. That turns out to be the case. Furthermore, I would remind the Court that during the course of this case many witnesses have discussed this issue and they have uniformly stated that it is impossible to distinguish between Serbs, Muslims and Croats by facial features. Indeed, the accused himself at pages 44 and 58 of his May record of interview says the same thing. But now despite the fact that Dr. Wagenaar's concerns are wholly alleviated, Mr. Wladimiroff insists on this new issue.
