This effort to impose both an hypertechnical and unfounded standard on a valid test epitomizes the Defence attack on valid procedures which yielded highly probative results. Mr. Wladimiroff also attacked witnesses for stating that they did not watch or read about events from former Yugoslavia or this trial. Apparently, he finds it hard to believe that people do not want to come home after a full day's work and settle in and watch stories about the events which destroyed their homes, killed members of their families and keep them awake at night with nightmares. I am not suggesting that there are not some people who may be drawn to such things, but I think logic and experience tell us it is extremely predictable that people would say, "I do not want to discuss this, I do not want to think about it, I know all I need to know about it". Indeed, that is part of the reason we have a Victims and Witnesses Unit here because victims have to come to the Court and discuss those very issues. Mr. Wladimiroff also suggests that Senad Muslimovic must have seen pictures of the trial since there was daily coverage of the trial by [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wonder just how likely it is that a Bosnian refugee with a low level job would pay good money to get a channel to watch lawyers argue in a foreign language. This kind of speculation by the Defence appears throughout their discussion on the subject. They insist, for example, that if Sead Halvadzic did not buy newspapers, he must have seen some photos on the street as he was walking by. They cite the number of references to Dusko Tadic in articles in [redacted]. (redacted). They could be about anything. They could be about Judge Goldstone, could be about the possibility of a permanent Tribunal, and so on. Furthermore, there was no information on the number of photos which appeared in those articles and, more importantly, there was no information on where in the newspapers those articles appeared, certainly no information about their appearance on the front page. I would also remind the Court that in the 80 plus articles which Mr. Deichmann submitted, which were allegedly examples of newspaper references to Tadic, at least 10 did not have any mention of the name "Tadic" in them at all. The Defence also read an extract or plucked an extract from the testimony of Kasim Mesic and asked the Court to focus on a particular portion of that extract. I simply want to remind the Court about this witness, if you recall him, and he was an older man who clearly was not finding being a witness in Court and communicating very easy. He struggled to make clear what he was saying about the procedures. Even beyond that, however, even if one were to apply a completely mechanical interpretation of what he said, it is clear there was no meaningful transgression of the procedures, and that he was relating basically that he was told or asked to look at these photographs and see if he could recognise a subject. Just one mention about the witness Draguna Jaskic in case there is any lingering confusion about that. She was just shown one photospread. Then later you heard from an investigator about her reaction during the course of viewing the photographs in that photospread. You heard her explain to you what that reaction was about. Perhaps it is best just to cut to the chase on this issue. The reason we do not have eyewitnesses come to court and simply tell us whether the person in court is the individual who committed the crime, according to Dr. Wagenaar, is that it is relative easy to figure out in court who the accused is. This lowers the probative value, but does not eliminate it, according to him. So it is prudent to make reasonable efforts to reduce the possibility that some deduction or guessing may be involved. Dr. Wagenaar also pointed out that there are certain witness who fall into a category with some special significance. Those are people who did not know the accused before they saw him at the place where the crime was committed and, therefore, if they can pick him out of a group of similar looking people, the only logical explanation is that the accused was at the scene of the crime. As Judge McDonald correctly noted, Dr. Wagenaar indicated that violations of his recommended procedures did not invalidate a photospread or a test; it simply made it more difficult for the Court to conduct its job of weighing the evidence. He talked about looking for -- I think his quote was -- "really gross violations". We were provided some examples of really gross violations by Dr. Wagenaar based on an article he had written in 1990. I will not go through all those with you. Let me just recount a few of those factors: Perpetrators wearing a full mask, with a one person line up, every foil different in some significant way from the accused with a small lineup size, perhaps three or four, a lineup of three people with the suspect the only person in distinctive clothing, witnesses talking to one another during the course of a lineup, witnesses being told that the suspect was in the lineup and suggestions to witnesses to change their identifications. The Court can find all the rest of those at 5842 through 43. You can be certain that you will never find on a list of really gross violations a photo lineup procedure and photo lineup of the type that was used here. I remind the Court that we heard from Mr. Reid not about procedures in general but the procedures that were used for the identification witnesses who testified in this case. This is what it involved. There were 13 photos, more than twice the acceptable number, a photospread which was subjected to the Doob and Kirschenbaum test and approved, witnesses asked to look carefully at the photographs and if they recognised anyone to so indicate. I should note that Dr. Wagenaar initially suggested that the absence of an explicit instruction saying that the witness -- suspect might not be in the photo lineup could be a problem, but he later acknowledged that studies simply indicated that there was a difference between situations where the witnesses were told that the suspect might not be in the lineup and where witnesses were told affirmatively that he was. He had nothing in particular to say about a situation where neither instruction was given as here. No photo was shown here to a witness for a longer or shorter time than others. In fact, the witnesses controlled the photo book. They were handed it and they perused it. The selection of the photos was immediate. There was no lengthy deliberation. The entire process from instruction to signing the back of the photograph took approximately three minutes in all cases. The witnesses expressed certainty at the identification. None of the foils were selected. There was no repeated testing. The witnesses were alone. They were not told to look more carefully at one photo than another. They were not given feed back about their choice and the sequence of the accused's photo in the photo lineup was changed for each witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Tieger, I think that Judge Stephen is right in his questions that he has raised before, without casting any aspersions on Mr. Reid, that his testimony was conclusory and no indication that he was there when this test was being administered. The Defence, I imagine, if they wish to challenge the procedures before Dr. Wagenaar testified, could have called the people who actually conducted the test; or if it is incumbent upon the Prosecutor, the Prosecutor could have called the people who actually conducted the test other than Mr. Paepen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Reid is the chief investigator who supervises the conduct of the entire investigation and the performance of the investigators who conduct these photo lineups in the course of the investigation and his information, I would call it not conclusory, it was based on ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I said conclusory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I am sorry, your Honour. It was based on the information he received from the investigators relating to each and every identification. I remind the Court that part of the purpose of doing so is the Prosecution has an obligation to disclose exculpatory evidence. Mr. Reid has to determine whether there is a problem with the identification and he has to discuss that with the investigators both for the purpose for which he appeared in court and for that reason as well. He is conducting a highly important task and he is aware of it. One final point on this subject. Because Dr. Wagenaar suggested that it might be helpful for the Court to know whether or not there were other photo identifications conducted, so you would know whether or not these were only four of 100 and the other 96 failed and these might be the results of guessing, the Prosecution produced evidence of all those tests. Now we find that Mr. Wladimiroff complains that the Prosecution did not produce those witnesses and he was not allowed to cross-examine them. It is beyond me why he is complaining that there is not more evidence in this case, and I also remind the Court that Dr. Wagenaar himself testified specifically that four people was plenty. He finds any more identification witnesses needless. But then Mr. Wladimiroff goes on to speculate that the Prosecution must not have produced these witnesses because there was something wrong with the identification. If this is the only reason he can think of, it is rather surprising coming from someone who has complained about the difficulties in getting even non-traumatized witnesses to Court. This kind of speculation should be disregarded. In any event, if Mr. Wladimiroff had a problem with that, the Defence could have cross-examined Mr. Reid about the procedures used with those other witnesses. Certainly no basis for any suggestion that any procedure other than the one used for the four witnesses mentioned would have been employed or that it was any different. During argument, Mr. Wladimiroff asked rhetorically where the picture of Dusko Tadic painted by Miss Hollis in her closing address originated from. He wondered whether it was simply the stereotypical image of a Serb. I am not sure I know exactly what that stereotypical image is supposed to be, but I do know that Miss Hollis' closing address was a detailed recitation of the evidence. The image of the defendant which emerged from her closing address was based on the defendant's deeds and on the defendant's words. The Defence asked how can anyone call the accused a fanatic, although I think the Defence was the first to raise that term, simply because he ran a local plebiscite. Miss Hollis has already addressed the significance of both the plebescite to Serbs as well as the lies the accused told about that plebiscite. But, in any event, that is far from the only evidence which bears on this issue. Just to name a few, the accused is the man who worked at gathering weapons before the war, organised war assignments, attempted to get intelligence on the number and nature of weapons possessed by the legitimate police, discouraged Serbs from participating in joint activities with Muslims, angrily told a neighbour in Kozarac, "This will be greater Serbia, it will all be ours and Muslims will not be there any more".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Where do you get the information regarding the prior acts, not the angrily telling the neighbour? I know that is Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is out of the work report, your Honour, and in the materials we provided I believe there is specific reference to the page numbers of the report on which that appears. By "work report", of course, I am referring to the report prepared by the accused on his work for the SDS between 1990 and 1993. The accused is also the man who told a Muslim reserve police officer, "You will all disappear from here". He is the man who at home, when the mask was slightly down, called Muslims by derogatory epithets "balijas". I ask the Court just to put that in whatever context is appropriate for you and that illuminates fully what someone reveals when he speaks about a member of any national, religious, racial or ethnic group and says, "Look at the blank going to church or synagogue or shrine reason or whatever". The accused is also the man who boasted how he liberated Kozarac to Mirsad Blazevic. The accused is a self-described SDS activist and enthusiastic supporter of the creation of Republika Srpska even when it meant risking his life. That is out of the work report as well. That is the accused's own words. He is also a participant in the cleansing assaults and murders of Muslims in opstina Prijedor. The Defence remind the Court about some of the evidence concerning the political philosophy of the SDS and there was considerable, particularly in the early stages of the case, but assert that none of this has been connected in any way with the accused because he professes never to have read political tracts. First of all, there is an obvious connection. The accused is an "earnest member" of the SDS. To understand what that means, one must understand the philosophy of both the Serbs past and present, as we now do. The philosophies articulated by Cubrilovic and Moljvic, the expulsion of non-Serbs, was echoed by Radoslav Brdjanin in Banja Luka, the Head of the Krizni Stab, who said that there would only be two per cent non-Serbs in what was to be Republika Srpska, and as you heard from Vasif Gutic who was also echoed locally by Slobodan Kuruzovic. You have seen those articles and the language and the nature of the SDS philosophy. To suggest that someone who is a member of that group does not understand the nature of the ideals which are embodied in that group defies logic, and again asks the Court to put it in appropriate context. The other day Miss Hollis used an analogy with the Ku-Klux-Klan -- I think a dozen groups which would suffice. I do not think anyone could credibly suggest that anyone who had not read political tracts by leaders of that group would not know what the group stood for. The Defence ignores all that. They try to suggest that the accused's involvement in the League for Peace stands in contradistinction to that, that he was selected because he was regarded as a man of peace. We know that he was selected because, as we heard from the members of that group, they did not want to have a monoethnic group and they wanted to be sure they could get past the Serbian checkpoints, and having a Serb with them was the best way to achieve that. We heard about the work report yesterday from Miss de Bertodano. I think little needs to be said about the Defence effort to characterise that work report. It may be a pathetic document, but it is also an extremely revealing one. If the Defence does not acknowledge that, certainly the accused does. On page 6150 of his testimony he noted that, "A lot of documents that you have offered here in evidence against me were found with those papers", by that he means in Germany. "If I had thought about that, I would have never have taken them with me to Germany". With regard to what the defendant or the accused knew at the time he was writing that about allegations against him, in general, I point the Court specifically to page 6149 in which the accused discusses the information he had at the time. He had read some information in the Serbian paper. He linked the Monika Gras's visit in January '93 to himself and he knew that it concerned activities in Kozarac. That stands in addition to the information discussed yesterday about the conversation he had concerning the paper in Zagreb with Nikola Petrovic. Beyond that, the fact is that everybody knows this kind of information cannot get out. The fact is that the accused had, as the intended recipients of this work report, the media in former Yugoslavia, not just Serbian leaders. I think we can see the reluctance to discuss even the most minor aspects or involvement with the crimes of opstina Prijedor in the kind of "see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil" attitude we saw from many of the Defence witnesses in Court. I want to address one last point and that is Miss de Bertodano's assertion that the accused should be credited because he has told the same story from the start. The Defence says, well, he is not tailoring his testimony. In fact, I think they said that his memory just got better over time. That is a memory principle I did not hear Mr. Kay express when he was discussing the Prosecution witnesses, but be that as it may, we can ask the question, is it possible for people to remember things on an earlier occasion that they did not recall? Sure, of course it is. Does that, however, explain what happened here? A look at the evidence indicates it clearly does not. Miss de Bertodano gives as an example the accused's alleged realisation that his first day of work was not 17th, as he had previously stated in May 1995 and again in December 1995, but actually the 16th. She told us that memory was sparked by the documents showing dates and times. That is why when he came to Court he had a different version. That is what the accused told us in Court, but that is not what the evidence shows. We have Exhibit 361. It was introduced into evidence. It is a list of all the dates and times which the accused worked, June, July, August. It is much easier to read than the rosters themselves. You can measure it against the rosters. At least for June or July, which I am familiar with, it is completely accurate. The Defence wants you to believe, and has asserted, that even though he had it with him, he disregarded it, he did not use it. Again Miss de Bertodano had no choice because that is what the accused said on the stand, but that is not what the evidence shows. You heard from Miss Hollis how the accused actually used the document and changed on the same date from saying he was not on duty to giving the specific time he was on duty after referring to this document. There are other things that the accused said about June 16th contrary, which is the date he said in his May and December interviews that he was mobilized but did not serve, despite the fact that that date shows him on duty at the checkpoint, according to the rosters, and he says he was not on duty. How does he remember that in his interviews? He says that as he was leaving the police station that day -- there is a very detailed description of the events of that day -- he remembered that he was given his military book and in that book there was the stamp for that day which showed his mobilization. That stamp is June 16th and it is the same date that appears in military book which is in evidence. If I may, let me just take a brief look at this same story the accused has supposedly been telling from the start, the story which, as you heard from the Defence, is repeated in virtually all details -- that was the phrase they used -- by his principal alibi witnesses, his wife and his brother. What I particularly want to emphasise is not simply the change in accounts, although those are certainly substantial enough to undermine any notion of alibi, but also the way in which they reflect an obvious attempt to match stories. Going through them quickly (and these are just some of them and I realise we have time concerns and I want to leave Miss Hollis sufficient time), the accused said when he was first interviewed about this particular subject that his family left Kozarac in April '92, first left Kozarac in April '92, he and his family with the priest, and returned at the end of April. Mira Tadic then testified in court ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you give us a page on that of the interviews? We might read the entire two interviews, but it would make it easier. As you go through them, if you can give us, if you are going to give any more?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would be happy to.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Or, as we had indicated to Mr. Kay, you can read the transcript and then give us the cites after you have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have some of them on other pages.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Those you do not have, you may substitute later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I said, he first said in his interview that he and his family left Kozarac with the priest in April and returned at the end of April. Then Mira Tadic testified that the family left on April 1st and there was no priest involved. The accused testified afterwards that, indeed, they left at the beginning of April and there was no priest involved. The accused said in his record of interview that Mira Tadic came back from Kozarac with him the next morning. Then she testified that instead she had gone on to Kozice, as you heard, and did not come back to Kozarac. So the accused testified and said, "Mira Tadic went on to Kozice and did not come back". In fact, they both say he drove her and the family to Kozice. The accused said in his record of interview that in the first week of May Ljubo drove the family to Banja Luka. Then Mira Tadic testified that in the first week of May, on May 3rd specifically, the whole family, including the accused, left with the priest for Banja Luka and returned to Kozarac after a few days. So the accused testified that on May 3rd the whole family went to Banja Luka with the priest and returned to Kozarac after a few days. Miss de Bertodano also recounted for the Court how the accused was in Kozarac for one day at the beginning of June and then overnight during the second week with a trip to Trnopolje in between. She said specifically that in all of his interviews, and she identified those, the one German and the two Prosecution interviews, he spoke of visiting Kozarac, going to his family home or in Banja Luka. But, in fact, it is not what the accused did. After telling the German authorities that he was never in Kozarac between the time he left just before the war and returning to join the traffic police, they continued to press on the point. They were very insistent on that point. When he said he did not return during that time period, they said, "I am now asking you expressly, during this period of time were you only in Banja Luka and nowhere else?" and he said, "I was only in Banja Luka". He later said that he slept there every night and, to keep that story consistent, he related that he did not go to Trnopolje until after he joined the reserve police. He did not go to Trnopolje until late June. Other differences in this version can be found at pages 63 through 68 and page 78 of the May record of interview, but I will submit that as a whole package.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tadic have an attorney at that time with the German authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that indicated in the record of interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it is indicated directly in the record of interview and also by Mr. Huebel. It is also indicated, I might add, in the motion submitted by the Prosecution in connection with the admissibility of this matter which was supported by declarations and that issue was extensively addressed in that motion. After it was addressed, the Court may recall, the Defence withdrew its motion. In a similar manner, Miss de Bertodano, in support of the position that the story has always been the same, reminds the Court that we have talked about uniforms during the course of this case, and again in all three interviews the accused talks about them. In each one she said, "We hear about the camouflage clothes given by Ljubo". Again that is not the case. In his German interview again, he was specifically asked whether he had a camouflage or other military uniform or whether he had ever worn one. The accused said, "No, no, as far as the camouflage uniform is concerned". He just had a blue police uniform which he wore at the checkpoint. The Defence attempts to explain this. They say he did not consider the uniform that his brother gave him a proper uniform. If that was not considered a proper uniform, then we have to ask who gave him the uniform that he then talks about in his May record of interview when he says that during June 1992 he was in a multi-coloured uniform? Again I will supply the Court with citations which indicate the progression of this account. Miss Hollis did address in her closing address the time period between June 15th and June 18th. I invite the Court to look very carefully at the accused's description of this and compare it to that provided by Mira Tadic, in particular. I would simply note in supplementing that that the accused goes on to talk about 19th and 20th, and throughout that entire period there is no mention of Mira Tadic, which is strikingly in contrast with her testimony and in contrast with the accused's testimony in Court. I should also note that the origin or at least the beginning of this effort to co-ordinate stories began when the accused was in prison and sent a letter to his wife. That is under circumstances where he knew his letters would be read. The prisoners had to submit letters in unsealed envelopes to be mailed because they were going to be read before being mailed, so he tried to bury information to Mira Tadic in that letter. What he said was in Exhibit 354(b): "We have been divorced since 1985 and have only been seeing each other once in a while. Remember that we spent each night together from 15th to 20th June 1992. I worked for the traffic police in Prijedor. I hope you will be able to testify." There was also discussion about the certificate which we have heard much about, the certificate issuing Mr. Tadic an automatic rifle and 300 rounds of ammunition on May 4th. That is Exhibit 148. Miss de Bertodano acknowledges that that certificate was discussed and that the accused's answer was, "I did not receive any weapons". She says that the accused's answer was, "I did not receive any weapons from the staff of the Territorial Defence." That is not entirely correct. The full answer was, "I know nothing about it". Only then does he go on to deny its contents. This is in a context where all the questions and answers are interpreted to the accused before they go on to the next one. So what on earth was the accused referring to as "it" if not the certificate which is explicitly referenced in the German interview as you will see immediately before the question and answer, and in which the question is, "What can you tell us about that certification?" Miss de Bertodano noted that there was a witness who testified about that and said there was some question about whether or not documents had been produced to Mr. Tadic, and asserted that the witness's answer was, "Well, they were always produced" but he was not specific about this case. I do not know how this witness could have been more specific. He said at page 6440, "We did show that document to Mr. Tadic. He did have an opportunity to see it and become acquainted with it". He then said basically the same thing three more times, and that the last time he was actually holding the certificate as he was saying, "We gave him the opportunity to look at the document, to read it and Mr. Tadic did see the document and Mr. Tadic could read the document. He was granted the time and possibility to do so". The defendant knew that was not a good answer.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tadic testify, though, that he had not seen the certificate?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, he did, your Honour. He testified specifically he had not seen the certificate.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because I asked, I think Miss de Bertodano a question about that. I did not really remember whether he had said he had not seen it or whether there was just some confusion about it. OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the accused appreciated early that that was a problem. So, in May 1995, when Mr. Reid was talking to him about weapons he had, in speaking about his automatic rifle he said, "Oh, and as far as this weapon goes, I went to Prijedor and I got a blank certificate from a reserve military personnel named Slobodan Bokan and I filled it in at the beginning of May." Again I will provide you with the cite for that. That turns out to be something of a problem for the accused, as even Miss de Bertodano noted, because the certificate says the "Banja Luka Territorial Defence" which is something of a coincidence because, indeed, the accused was in Banja Luka on May 4th and is even a greater coincidence because, as you may recall from Exhibit 145, there was a general mobilization in the autonomous region of Krajina from Banja Luka on May 4th. So the next thing that happens is that Ljubomir Tadic comes to court and he takes credit for giving the accused a certificate. He says that happened in June when they were coming back from a trip to Kozarac. He says he filled it out. Of course, this is troublesome because the accused has said he already had a certificate. So, finally, the accused comes to court and says, "Oh, well, I had two certificates, one from Ljubo and one from Prijedor", except that, unlike Ljubo, he has actually seen the certificate and he knows the date on the certificate. So he says, unlike Ljubo, that the certificate was filled out on May 4th, the date on the certificate, and that he filled it out -- the same story from the start. There are a list of other movements, shifts, alterations of the accused's version. I would urge the Court to look, for example, at the accused's testimony 6068 through 6069 and compare it to his December interview at pages 23 to 24 for a change in his story about Witness W, after Witness W came in and denied being part of the conflict in Kozarac; for a change in his story about Milan Vlacina at page 6071 through 72, in contrast to his May interview on page 67 and the December interview on pages 13, 15 and 20; also for a change in the accused's story about sleeping in a camping caravan at the Orlovci checkpoint, after Miroslav Brdar came in and said, "No, no, we never slept at the caravan, in fact, there was no caravan". You can find that in the December interview at page 60 and the testimony of the accused at page 6075. Finally, I would direct the Court, as it occurs to me now, to an interesting section in the work report that has not been discussed. In that work report the accused says the following on page 11: "Not to this day was I able to understand who needed all that and what it was all about, because I had spent time on reserve duty more than seven months while they who insisted so much in persecuting me never did more than two months, more than seven months". June 16th to, let us say, mid December or late December which, I believe, is the date that appears in the accused's military book, is just a little more than six months. But it is more than interesting that if you count back to May 4th, to that December date, you have a time period which is in fact more than seven months. I invite the Court to make that comparison.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not understand that. What is the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The May 4th document, your Honour, indicates a mobilization which would be considered the beginning of a kind of service, even though someone might not be active at the time. The accused has told the Court that his mobilization, in fact, did not begin until he started with the reserve police on June 16th. In the work report he asserts that he was, in fact, on reserve status for more than seven months.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you count from May?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The May document does give him a weapon and ammunition, in fact, 300 rounds of ammunition, as a soldier. I find that an extremely interesting comment by the accused in his work report which certainly tends to confirm the significance of that certificate.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I guess I do not want to prolong it, but what was the date of the work report?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He wrote the work report in August 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So if you count from when to when you get more than seven months?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The end of his service, as reflected in his military book, was December 25th. So there appears to be a discrepancy which might not seem that significant otherwise between June 16th and December 26th which is just a little over six months. However, and it might not be that noteworthy if you did not have the document showing that he was issued a rifle and ammunition as a soldier on May 4th, and, what, coincidentally, that is in fact more than seven months as he asserts he served in the work report.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does Mr. Tadic deny being mobilized on May 4th?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I suppose I have missed that. There is in evidence a military book?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is a military book in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you know the Exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: D8, your Honour. I might also remind the Court, you may wish to take a look at Exhibit 150 which are the minutes of a meeting of the Kozarac local committee in which Dusko Tadic and Milenko Zigic are appointed to be in charge of issues pertaining to military records. Your Honour, unless the Court has some questions, I thank the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I will try to make my points very quickly and very directly. Mr. Tieger has touched on the details of the photographic lineups for the four identification witnesses and some of the Defence issues in those. The Defence, of course, spent much discussion on identification witnesses. It is, perhaps, helpful to make some general points that Mr. Wagenaar made for you concerning recognition or identification issues, if you will. Judge Stephen, I believe you were the one who asked Dr. Wagenaar, "What if a person comes in much after the fact and says, 'I saw a person with a moustache or a beard or without a moustache or beard' or 'I saw them in a uniform of a certain kind'? Is that certain a person would remember?" I think it is helpful here when we look at this in the context of the Defence argument to take a look at what Dr. Wagenaar told you. Basically, he told you that if a person, as to moustache or beard, if you know a person and you are accustomed to seeing them either with or without, then your memory maybe with or without and that may be incorrect, as far as facial hair is concerned, but that is of no significance to the fact that you saw them when you say you saw them. He indicated something very interesting as to identification witnesses, that if they say, "At the time I saw this individual he had facial hair", and then they are shown a photographic lineup where he does not have facial hair, then, in fact, you have built in an additional test into that book. Because if they can recognise him without facial hair when before they saw him with facial hair, that is another indicia of the reliability of the identification and makes it even less likely that it would be chance. As far as the uniforms are concerned, the doctor said, "If you are in an area where everyone wears uniforms and then several years later you are asked to describe someone, you may put them in a uniform you saw, even though perhaps they were wearing something different". I am sure that once the Court heard that, they wished that perhaps we had put Dr. Wagenaar on at the beginning of our case and it would have, perhaps, cut down on some of the questions we had asked our witness, because indeed you have heard a great deal about uniforms in this case. But we would also point out to you that when you look at the Defence evidence the accused had many types of uniforms, including a multi-coloured greenish brown shirt or jacket that he wore including this yellow, brown, light jacket. You recall the witness from Omarska who said he had a giraffe skin colour uniform on, and perhaps there is a linkage there. There have been discussions about black uniforms in Sivci. If you recall, Subha Mujic, she said it was black, camouflage black, camouflage blue. You will recall that you had evidence before you that, in fact, police wore this blue, dark blue camouflage uniform. So a great deal of attention has been spent to uniform. Dr. Wagenaar tells you a person could see someone they knew, recognise them accurately and later transpose an image of a uniform on to them when, in fact, the person did not have.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, also if you are making reference to the testimony, would you please when you receive the transcript provide us with the transcript cites?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we certainly will. As for the significance of facial hair, your Honour, that would be 5767 and 68 and 5857 and 58. There is another area concerning recognition that we need to look at that Dr. Wagenaar talked to you about, and that was the issue, if you know a person and you recognise them, what would you remember about it? You recall that in regard to recognition Dr. Wagenaar told you that human beings are somewhat unique in that they seem to have hard wired into their brains the ability to recognise and remember faces. This is something they will recognise and remember even when other details may become blurred or forgotten. "I will never forget that face" is a term people use and perhaps it has a great deal more significance than we think it does. In any event, he also indicated that when a person is looking at a face that it is a global picture that they have. They do not remember minor details. He told you that you can know someone very well and not be able to describe minor details. He said you would have some sort of broad description, and that would include something about height and size, but he said you have to give great parameters there because humans differ greatly in their ability to judge that, and hair colour. Samir Hodzic testified in this case and there was an issue about a prior statement where he described the accused's hair colour. You will recall there that he indicated in the prior statement that "it was light" was the translation. You will recall in this courtroom he described that it was "light going to dark" and described that he what he meant was perhaps "sunlightened hair, light coming off the sun". There, I believe, we have an indication this is a person who could remember the general details of a person he said he knew. The fact that he could remember the general details only is not inconsistent with his knowing this person. When you look at the potential inconsistency between his prior statement and the statement that he gave you in this courtroom under oath, you should keep in mind the problems that we have with translation and interpretation. You recall throughout this trial, where we have highly qualified people working as interpreters, we have had difficulties with interpretation. The Defence yesterday chose to mention that Zemka Sahbaz perhaps should not be believed because she at one point said that the accused was in a blue camouflage uniform. You will recall on the record that that was corrected. That was a translation error. In fact, she had said "green" but it was translated as "blue". That was corrected on the record for you. I will provide you with the page cite. These things have happened. You will recall in a perhaps more sombre note an occasion where someone was talking about a child that had been pierced with a pitchfork and initially came out as "pierced with rags", again because of unfamiliarity with a term and because of translation concerns. In regard to prior statements, when you are assessing these potential inconsistencies, we ask you to keep in mind that the interpreters used in other circumstances may not be as highly skilled as the interpreters we have here, and that could cause more problems. In addition to that, you will remember that when Elvir Grozdanic testified, he was also questioned about his prior statement. He was questioned about a section of it where he had talked about seeing these men as he came out of a restaurant, and seeing people in the statement he had opined to be Fikret Harambasic and Emir Karabasic. When he came into this courtroom, because he was here before you in a judicial setting, he chose not to opine about who those men were. Somehow, this was attacked to make it appear as though he were being less truthful with you or trying to change his story. I suggest to you what he was trying to do was to be more accurate in the detail he was giving you because of the seriousness of these proceedings. At any rate, he indicated that in the statement he had given before, when he was telling about this injured person being taken off in a wheelbarrow, the interpreter did not, apparently, know the word for "wheelbarrow" so in the statement it had the person being take off in a "wheelchair" when, in fact, it was a wheelbarrow. Again these are not made to cast any apersions on interpretation, simply to indicate that this is a fact that this Tribunal has had to deal with. You certainly will have inconsistencies or potential inconsistencies to deal with, and you will have to resolve them. We ask that you look very carefully at what was said, though, in resolving them and that you check very carefully what both the Prosecution and the Defence tell you are inconsistencies. I would like to speak for a moment about some of the inconsistencies that were pointed out to you yesterday by the Defence. In the initial opening remarks, Mr. Jos Paepen was mentioned again in a very unfavourable light. It was indicated that in regard to Draguna Jaskic's statement about her reaction, why she had reacted, that the Defence said it was her alleged reactions because the only information they had about that was her own statement, and the additional information from a witness who was an inexperienced law enforcement officer. They went on to say, "I say inexperienced because he had never performed a photo test before." If we go to Mr. Paepen's testimony at page 2980, what do we find out about what he said about his experience in showing photo lineups? The question put to him was, "Is this the first time you have been involved in a photo identification through the book?" referring to the one shown to Draguna Jaskic. "With this book, yes, sir, but in this case it was the first time I did". "Is that the only occasion you have been involved with a photo identification in this case?" "Yes, sir, it is". Somehow that got transformed into this was the first time he ever showed a photo lineup. It is important to look very carefully at what the witness has said and what the evidence says to ensure that, given the volume of this information, something has not been unknowingly, unintentionally misstated. If we turn to Witness Q (and you are certainly going to have to deal with Witness Q), there were several allegations made about Witness Q and his believability. In making these allegations and discussing the credibility of this witness, the Defence counsel asked some questions. He asked such things as, well, between 24th May when Q says he saw the accused in Kozarac and 26th May which was the next sighting, where was he, what was he doing? I suggest to you that the Serb church and the priest's house were not hit at all by shells, and that would have been terrific place for this accused to remain while he was waiting to take on his next duties. I also suggest that this accused at this time was not acting as a civilian interloper in Kozarac. He had been mobilized. He was in the military. He was a person familiar with the town. The people in the town, if they saw him, would not be unduly alarmed to see him there even during the shelling because, you remember, they continued to frequent his cafe even when the situation was very tense. He was brought there by the military. He was inserted there by the military. It was the Serb forces who were controlling the shelling. There were lulls in the shelling. That is when he was put in. Why would you be sending people in this way and putting them at risk of being hit by shells, and why on earth would the artillery not have had the correct sightings? People that are familiar with the military know that artillery officers are not as good as they say they are; and why would you put someone in to fire flares? You might put this accused in to fire flares? For one thing, because he wants to assist in the takeover; for another thing, because the flare is going to help ensure that his home and cafe are not damaged. You recall from Azra Blazevic that, in fact, when she went down the road on 26th May there was damage in Kozarac, but the accused's home and cafe had incidental damage you would expect from shelling close to it, windows knocked out and things like that. No indication from her that his home was ever hit by a shell. So perhaps that is why he was there; that is what he was doing there. The church incident that the Defence talks about in regard to Witness Q, and they indicate to you that the church incident derives from his testimony and that young children who had been standing guard duty near the Serb orthodox church came to complain to Witness Q. Then later he indicates that there was a man called Besic on duty, but Q confirmed to me he did not actually speak to Besic. He spoke to another adult and again says this sighting is by children. You recall it was Q who used the word "children". At page 1546 he was asked about the age group. He is talking about youngest and oldest at the hospital, and he says approximately 17 years of age up to about 45. He talks about people who came to him to tell him about the incident at the church. Then on page 1548 he says that one chap came and that immediately then they went to the church area to find out what had happened, and that at the church there was this older man, Besic, and the rest of the children who were guarding the church. He says, yes. Then the question is: "This Besic did not come to speak to you?" He said, "No, that is correct". Then Q tells us, "The first story that something had happened down there was told by a child and only a very small part. The rest of the story was told by the rest of those people who remained there, and those were those children and this elderly man, Besic, that I mentioned". So, in fact, he spoke to this adult, this elderly man Besic -- although I believe he said elderly was 45 -- and, in fact, he was the one who confirmed that story for him. The Defence also attacked Witness Q saying that he used the hospital because there was such emotive connotations to use the hospital as an example. Azra Blazevic told you there was very heavy shelling on the night of 24th and morning of 25th, and that, in fact, the hospital was hit that night and there were wounded people there. So this is not a fabrication to appeal to your emotion. The Defence also indicates, well, these extreme allegations that he talked about, this child killed by a pitchfork, a man stuck against the door, these are extreme allegations trying to prejudice the Court. We ask you to consider the other evidence in this case, the castration of Fikret Harambasic was truly an extreme measure, but it happened. Mustafa Mujkanovic told you of having to bury dead people while he was in Trnopolje, including his brother. He told you about that, that he found his brother, his eldest brother, stabbed five times in the chest, one of his breasts, he called it, cut off and he said, "I apologise, but I have to say his genitals were cut off and he was also slashed over his throat". Perhaps people might say that Mr. Mujkanovic made that up also trying to appeal to your prejudices. I suggest you would not make up that sort of destruction invited upon a member of your family. Extreme measures happened, extreme crimes were committed. Again in regard to Witness Q, the Defence indicated that at Keraterm he claimed to have been able to see Dusko Tadic at some considerable distance away. If we look at the testimony of Witness Q at page 1573, he says that he was in cell No. 2. He said that what would happen is that information would be passed from one person to another. He told you that his normal place was in the back of the room. He said that what happened was people that he believed would know the accused, people from Kozarac, said, "Here comes Tadic". What did he tell you then happened? He told at 1581, "I was still in my corner. The news that I heard was that Dusko arrived. I simply moved from my position to the large wall and I glanced towards the exit doors and this is where I saw him. After that I immediately went back to my place." Then he tells you that he heard again when the accused was leaving, and so he again came forward to look; again the point being it is very important to look at what the witnesses have said. Turning to Azra Blazevic, the Defence speaks of her in terms of a brief fleeting glance of a lady convinced it was the accused because of a remark made at the time, someone saying it was Dusko Tadic. Let us look, first of all, at what she had to say about what convinced her. At page 1626 she said that she heard someone say, "There is Dule", and that she looked up because it meant that somebody they knew was there. She looked around and she noticed Dusko Tadic crossing the street not far away. She was asked if there was anything about the incident that made her sightings stick out in her mind. She said that it remained in her mind "because Nihad Bahonjic was not taken from the intersection with us to Trnopolje, and all the time after that we were wondering why he was taken and who took him, because the soldier that came and called out Nihad Bahonjic called him out by his name and last name. None of us knew the soldier and I remember the only known face, the only person that we knew and who was there and that was Dusko Tadic." She says, "I do not believe I was mistaken because at that moment when I looked around me, looking for a familiar place, I was not looking to see the accused but simply the person that was crossing the street." Dr. Wagenaar tells you something about these fleeting glances. He tells you about them in the context of a person who does not know the individual they are looking at and in the context of a recognition witness, such as Mrs. Blazevic was. He said the second situation where you have a recognition witness recognising a person that you know is done much more quickly. It can be done within a second that you say, "Ah, he, that is him." It can take from zero to any time after that. In fact, a quick recognition is what you would expect from someone who knows the person. That is found at pages 5846, and 5847. If a witness after two seconds says, "That's him" I would say that is totally acceptable." The Defence also talked about Nihad Seferovic who told you that he saw the accused commit crimes against two men in Kozarac on, he did not know. It was the day Kozarac surrendered. He thought it was a Tuesday. He did not know the date. Defence counsel said Seferovic who gave evidence about the church killings on the morning of 26th May, and went on to discuss that this was a problem for the Prosecution case because now we had the accused being here killing someone in the morning, being seen at the triangle by Q in the morning, being seen at Keraterm in the morning. Let us turn to Nihad Seferovic's testimony at 1770. "Can you remember what time of the day it was you went to go to your brother's house? It was in the early afternoon." Then if we go to 1773 the question is, "When you were going through the backyards and gardens, down to the orchard, after you had been to your brother's house, you said that you could see the church clearly? Yes, yes. It was not in the morning. It was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But did not S testify, was it S, that he saw the accused at Keraterm on that same day in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, ma'am, he testified that on 26th he saw the accused there after 10 o'clock in the morning. On 27th he said he saw the accused there in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well, you will provide the transcript cite once again.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe you have that in the materials already, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In the large volume?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. In regard to Nasiha Klipic the Defence, my goodness, she saw the accused coming from the direction of Prijedor, and by the way, this would have been on the day that Witness S said he saw him in Keraterm in the afternoon, and then she sees the accused coming from the direction of Prijedor passing her toward Kozarac, but then she is in this long column. She gets to the separation point and there he is. How did that happen? Judge Stephen indicated, well, perhaps there were cross-over points from the old road but I do not see on any map, I believe, sir, is what you indicated. We looked at Prosecution Exhibit 280. We have blown up that portion and, indeed, there are cross-over points and we do have the blown-up portions of that map available for you, if you wish, as well as for the Defence. So we suggest that is exactly what he did. He went that way. He came back along the old road. You will remember Witness V said that when they were moving into Kozarac at a junction around Kozarusa/Sujica somewhere they branched off, half his unit branched off, and went down the old road through Kozarusa, so that old road was controlled by the Serbs. He went in along the main highway, came back by the old road. He was in a car. No one was blocking him. That is how he was able to be there at the separation point for her to see him. Indeed, your Honour, Witness S with the two sightings is with the material you have under the Keraterm persecution count. The Defence also went back to clothing and made some comments about Sulejman Besic and Salko Karabasic saying that is it not peculiar that these two men said they saw the accused in a civilian suit. If we go to Mira Tadic's testimony at 4844 she talks about this summer camouflage uniform and says: "Can you describe it? What were the colours? It is a uniform that looks like a sports outfit, like a jump suit. You put it on top of your civilian clothes. It was beige, yellow, brown with spots." So a jump suit, casual clothes, it is not inconsistent with what these witnesses talked about, but they did believe it was camouflage. Indeed he was wearing this suit, it was camouflage, but it was of the yellow, brown, white colour camouflage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When the witness placed Mr. Tadic in civilian clothes, did he testify that it was multi-coloured?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was a prior statement about civilian clothes and in the courtroom they testified about camouflage type clothes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In the prior statement did he describe the civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If the statement was not introduced the question becomes whether it was elicited. So we will check the transcript. Did you give us the transcript cite for that?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The page for Mira Tadic was 4844.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Besic?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: For the prior statement?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When that is discussed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is in ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You can do it later.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I will submit that to you later. In regard to these two witnesses and the event that they testified concerning, I would express again that the Prosecution theory of that event was that the men that Ferid Mujcic saw being taken across the road were brought back. We know there was a lot of movement back and forth that day. We believe the explanation is the men were brought back. In regard to Judge Stephen's question about is it not true that the man behind, the man in the rear, was the one who said he also saw them brought out while the man who must have been in the middle said he did not, I would suggest you look very carefully at those portions of the testimony of Sulejman Besic. I believe there is some ambiguity there as to exactly where those men were at the point he saw him. I would also suggest that as this column went down that road, this huge column in this very traumatic and chaotic environment, that people were looking up and looking about at different times, and he behind Ferid Mujcic could very well have been looking forward and to the side and seen this occurring, while Ferid Mujcic did not see that as it happened, saw it when he looked just a bit later and saw them against the kiosk. I would suggest there is a reasonable explanation for what they saw of this event that occurred there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, in Counts 24 through 28 the Prosecutor charges that "Serb forces, including Dusan Tadic and Goran Borovnica, ordered", and then you name the people, "from the column and shot and killed them." If the Trial Chamber were to find that the evidence supported a finding that these people were called from the column but that the evidence did not support a finding that they were shot and killed, would that be a crime under any of the counts?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I think under Count 1, your Honour, because again it is assisting in the roundup of these people and their forced expulsion from Kozarac. In addition to that, your Honour, if you were to find that Ferid Mujcic's version was correct and Goran Borovnica had indeed struck one of them, I would suggest that the accused's presence there was not innocent presence, and he would be culpable in the striking of that civilian who had been called out as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As to coverage in Count 1, the Defence says that Counts 24 to 28 -- well, no, I guess not. That is May 27th and 11 and 12.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe they mention 29 to 34, your Honour, as not being included, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, 29 to 34 being June 14, therefore, after May 27th but this count is May 27th.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In regard to 29 to 34, your Honour, I believe paragraph 4 would include it because the time period there I believe is about 23 May until 31 December 1992. So I believe that is the general prefatory paragraph for the persecution count.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you about that then.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 says between 23rd May 1992 and 31st December 1992, and then you specify acts. Then 4.1 says between the dates of 24th, 27th May -- from the dates 24th to 27th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then in the last sentence you refer to paragraphs 11 and 12. The acts charged in 12 of course occurred on June 14th, that is what you charge, and then 11 that occurred on 27th. So you may not have a problem with paragraph 11, but what about 12? That goes beyond May 24th to May 27th. You are saying that paragraph 4 is the prefatory one?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. I believe when we set out the additional paragraphs there we were incorporating some other offences that may not have been specifically alleged, set out separately further on in the indictment, but I believe we did incorporate the offences we set out separately in the indictment. I believe they would be incorporated under that prefatory paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would that also apply to the beatings that were charged at the Prijedor barracks?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe we have a prefatory paragraph that addresses that. I believe there the issue is not so much if the -- I think you raised it yesterday perhaps in another context, and that would be in terms of if we had charged beatings at Prijedor barracks during a certain time period and the evidence proves that it was beatings at Prijedor barracks but perhaps a short time after the alleged time period, would that be a fatal variance in pleading such as to render it a more serious crime as to deprive the accused's notice so that he would not have been prepared to meet the charge. I would suggest that would be the issue there and that in these instances neither would be true. That, in fact, if we are talking about a time period that is toward the end of May and we have early June to 8th June, that that is close enough in time that it would be included. Secondly, I do not believe it would be fatal, because it is specific enough in what it alleges and the facts were specific enough so as to preclude a second trial for the same offence. It does not by the time difference make it a more serious offence, and the accused had sufficient information ahead of time through disclosure that he was able to defend against it. So I believe it would be included under the prefatory paragraph, and I do not believe there would be a fatal variance in the pleadings.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That was Judge Stephen's question I think, or at least one that related to timing. My question in terms of a fatal variance dealt with Counts 18 through 20 which I am sure you will address.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is correct. I believe it is the same principle you are talking about. In regard, your Honour, in regard 18 to 20, I think you are talking about the substance of acts, whereas here we are talking about the dates. I would suggest again there that using the same logic that is not a fatal variance, because what we are looking at, I believe, when we talk about a fatal variance is, is it such a difference that it would do one of three things: Number one, it would change the crime and make it more serious; number two, it would be so deficient that the accused would not be on notice of it so would not be able to prepare a defence against it, or, number three, that by changing it this way it would open up the possibility of a second trial for the same offence. Again, I believe because of the detail provided that that would not occur, even though what we had charged was the discharge of the nozzle of the contents of the fire extinguishers, and what the proves is shoving the hose into the person's mouth. Our position would be that is not a fatal variance for the reasons I stated. Your Honour, if we could move on now to some of the areas they talked about with Counts 5 to 11. They talked about Husein Hodzic and a prior statement of his. Again, I would ask that you look at the explanation and the circumstances of that prior Swedish statement they referred to in determining if, in fact, there is a significant inconsistency. The Defence talks about that prior statement in their cross-examination. I would suggest to you that if Husein Hodzic wanted to come in here and pin something on this accused there would have been a much more direct way to do that. That way would have been to come in here and say: "I was in that room that day. I heard Emir Karabasic called out. I heard what he said about Dule Tadic. I too went to that window and looked down into the hangar and I too saw Dule Tadic." But the witness did not testify to that. So either he is very subtle in his ways of pinning it on the accused, he is not bright enough to think of it or, in fact, he came in here and he testified to you about what he recalled of that date. We suggest that it is the latter explanation. As far as Emir Karabasic is concerned, the Defence said: Why did he say, "There he is"? Why did he not say, "There they are"? Why did he say those things? The evidence tells you why. He was afraid of this man. He had confirmed to Nihad Seferovic that he was among the group Nihad saw on the Tuesday, he thinks, when the surrender happened. He had not wanted to talk about details, but he had confirmed to Husein Hodzic that he his greatest fear was that the accused would come to that camp and would get him. There was discussion about how long he had been in the camp. We do not how long, but there is no indication in the record up until about five to seven days before this that the accused committed any of these crimes at Omarska inside the hangar. You recall Mr. Muslimovic testified that he first was beaten by the accused five to seven days before the 18th June incident, and that at that time the accused and the group followed him into the hangar, but only to that stairwell that went up to room 15. So had Emir Karabasic seen him in camp up until that time? Very likely not. Emir Karabasic had been beaten very badly. Was Emir walking around very much? Not likely. He looked down there and he saw the man he feared and that is why he said, "Dule is here, I am finished". That is why.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think that the Defence's position was that Mr. Tadic had an opportunity to see him earlier at the camp. This is June 18.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I do not know that anything says that a person is not guilty of a crime if they hold off until a later date. There is no indication as to why he waited until then. Many men were brought out that day, including Emir Karabasic. I do not believe the suggestion that he could have done it earlier overcomes the evidence that indeed he was there and did it on that day on 18th June. For the reasons I mentioned earlier, I do not believe that a reasonable conclusion is that Mr. Hodzic lied about what he heard on that date. They talked about Witness H who among the living, perhaps next to Meho Alic, is the one who was perhaps the most affected for the rest of his life by this incident. They talked about Witness H being there. They seem to indicate that the incident was the castration of Fikret Harambasic. That was certainly the most sensational part of that incident, but that was by no means the incident, because when Fikret Harambasic was emasculated by G five other men had already been severely, savagely victimized that day. When H went out there those acts had already been done. When we look at H's testimony what does he say about where he was looking and how he was looking when he went out? When H went out and when G went out do you think they were afraid of what was happening? I would suggest, yes, the reasonable inferences are that they were. He said on page 2649 that when he came out of the room he was looking down. He said when he saw Emir's body somebody asked: "Whom are we going to take?" He was looking down. He did not tell you who said that. He was asked: "Were you looking around in the garage and looking these soldiers?" He told you: "Only in so far as I could while we went up and down trying to pick up and drag Jasmin's body just for a moment." This is a witness that the Defence agrees is being truthful with you and is telling you how limited his ability to see everyone in that area was while he was out there. He also tells you after being pulled out of that canal he was put on his stomach with a knife at his eye and told to keep Fikret Harambasic's mouth closed or the knife would be used, and that while he was on his stomach someone put a foot on his neck and trampled him so that his chin and face were pushed into the floor of that hanger. He was not looking around at who was there when this was happening. If you look at his testimony we suggest that indeed his testimony does not preclude the presence of this accused at this time. He told you he did not see him and we believe that is 100 per cent accurate. That does not mean that the accused was not there. Senad Muslimovic supposedly lied about his testimony because there was this fellow Bakar or Bakan of some sort that had beaten Senad Muslimovic, and he should have known about it. I am sorry, your Honour, I am mixing up my people here. The issue about Senad Muslimovic was that he claimed that at the time he was being beaten by the accused Jasko Hrnic was also being beaten by the accused, and it therefore entered his mind. He links the two. Now at page 2536 he tells you how that scenario played out. He said he had been unconscious, he came too and he was not being beaten when he came too. At that time he saw Jasko Hrnic dragged over there and he saw the accused cutting him. He was not being beaten by the accused at that time. He saw the accused cutting this other man. Then he said a short time later he heard someone behind Muslimovic saying ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are having a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did I blow the transcript right off the screen! The interpreters want you to slow down, but we still have a problem with the transcript, it is not operative. Let me ask you this while the transcript is being repaired. How much longer do you have, Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will conclude at 1 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does the Defence -- you had indicated you did not have any rejoinder -- do you have any rejoinder and, if so, how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We may have altogether about a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will continue until both sides have finished then, expecting we will finish at 1.15, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to the extent my speaking too quickly causes I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, I have gone through the Defence argument and taken out many instances where I believe you need to look very carefully at the transcript and if you have no objection I would like to submit that to you as an aid, as a package, if you have no objection to that, and I will move on to other things.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection? There will be a list of transcript cites I gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, and it is what your Honour required of us in relation to our argument and we are in the process of doing anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good, thank you. That may be submitted.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is only one other person I want to speak of in relation to this incident, because I think it is particularly significant to this entire issue of whether all of these Prosecution witnesses have come in here out of revenge and have lied about what they saw. That is, when the Defence spoke of Meho Alic and they told you that: It is clear that he held back from saying he saw Dusko Tadic, he could not go further than saying, "I know he was there." They say that in terms of description he said: "I could not see them, who they were, what they were", and so he has held back from identifying Dusko Tadic at the scene, but he has gone into some other much more subtle way of trying to connect him with the crime. What we suggest to you is this, that if Maho Alic wanted to put the accused at the scene when his son was killed, he would have told you, "I saw him there." There was nothing to hold him back from that, nothing at all, except his own personal integrity. He did not see him there. So he came in here and he told you what happened as he knew it. He did not lie to you. Because he is an honest man who came here in the light of his tragedy he is an honest man. He told you no more and no less than what he saw and heard that day. We suggest that is true for the witnesses you have seen before you here, and that they did not come here as part of some bloodthirsty revenge to exact retribution against this accused for wrongs done to them. In regard to the Defence witnesses I would like to touch on a couple of those witnesses, and that is Mr. Brdar and Mr. Prpos. The Defence would you have you believe that these people are very important, and they are also very reliable. I would ask that you look very carefully at their testimony as well. If you look at Mr. Brdar what you will find, I suggest, is a man who came in here to give the image that everything worked perfectly at the checkpoint, that they were always on time, that they were always there, that they never slept. They had no trailer there in which to sleep, although other evidence says that is not true. He tells you that every day when they went to their shift, first they went to the police station, they reported in, they got the keys to the car, he drove them out to the shift and then they drove the car back in at the end of it. Now the man who ran the traffic section told you that, in fact, if there was a car they would come to the police station, otherwise they went directly there, but Mr. Brdar was very insistent that they always went to the police station to check in. Again, he is trying to make this much more perfect than it was, for what reasons, I do not know. Another factor to consider. Mr. Brdar, if the accused left there while he was on duty, do you think that Mr. Brdar would report him if it had no significant adverse impact on the functioning there? Judge Stephen asked: Why do we have three grown men at this checkpoint when, apparently, there are not that many civilian cars? I believe the evidence was that the military side which was very busy only had two people. I suggest Mr. Brdar would not have reported the accused's absence, number one, because it would not have affected what they were doing there, number two, because he would not want to be informing on someone he was working with and, number three, perhaps because he had no objections to what Mr. Tadic may have been doing when he was not there. Mr. Prpos also testified before you, and he testified about the accuracy of these records. He talked primarily about D66 and that was this log book, if you recall. Mr. Brdar I believe had indicated that really it was Mr. Prpos who filled that out and signed it and did all of this, but Mr. Prpos made it clear that his administrative clerk actually filled out many of those pages and signed Mr. Prpos's name to it. In fact, he tells you that at page 5215, at page 5218. At page 5217 when he was talking about this book and making up this book, on that page he said: "Yes, one can see from here", and he is talking about D66, "there is a certain equal rhythm if you look at the actual distribution. If a person works one day, then he does not work the next two days, for example." I suggest that is not a hypothetical. He is looking at this book, he is telling you very often what schedule may have been.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Slow down, Miss Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour. It is interesting to note that at page 5228 when he is talking about the accuracy of the book, he is asked at one point: "Is there any reason why we do not have a linking number here" and he is being shown a particular entry "which would correspond to the numbers within the official duty plan, the first book we look the at?" He says: "That is an error, an omission on the part of Cvijic who filled in this document." The next question is, interestingly: "Again, could you comment upon the accuracy of this document relating to the records of hours of duty for Dusko Tadic," and after telling you this is an error he said: "These records are accurate." Human beings made those records. There were inaccuracies in those records. That is proven when we look at the cross-examination of Mr. Vujanovic. During that cross-examination he was asked about these patrol warrants for Kozarac. These are Prosecution Exhibit 357. These are patrol warrants for September in Kozarac. Yesterday the Defence tried to say, well, there may have been some minor inconsistency there. Look carefully at those. There is not a minor inconsistency; there is a major overlap on one of them. Then they want to say, but, you know, Mr. Vujanovic he could not tell you anything about those patrol receipts, they were not his. Well, look at those patrol receipts and you are going to see a signature there, Dusko Tadic. He could tell you about them, he signed them. He said he was there when the record said he was somewhere else. Inaccuracies, they do exist in these records. The Defence in their argument has talked about Witness L and has wanted you to use what happened with Witness L to say that the entire Prosecution case is of absolutely no value because of that. We suggest that, in many ways, what happened with Witness L is certainly incredibly unfortunate and something that should never have happened, but in many ways it shows that the adversarial system works because the Defence had this man's name, they had the ability to investigate, they came up with information that was very relevant to this man, it was brought to the Court's attention and appropriate action was taken. I find it very interesting that the Defence says: This man is a liar, that has been proven, he is liar, but you know the one thing he is telling the truth about, the Muslims made him do it. Our position is this.
