He certainly lied about his family and we are not at all sure if he told the truth about anything else, but we are not at all sure, that is the point, because why would we automatically believe his last statement when all of the rest of his statements are in such serious doubt? Please recall the circumstances of that last statement. That last statement came out only after he had been alone with his father and brother who live in opstina Prijedor, and after that he said: "The Muslims made me do it." Also think about other information in this record, such as when the Defence counsel first brought the information about the family to this Court's attention, and you will recall how that was brought to your attention. It was indicated that during investigations in the area they happened almost by chance upon this family. How were they led to that family? Someone told them that a man by the name of Pero Opacic had been a guard at Trnopolje. Then when they found Pero Opacic, well, Pero Opacic is (redacted). knew things about the camp. What did he tell that was the truth, if anything, how much did he lie, we do not know. We indicated that we would investigate the matter. We began an investigation. We have initial results from that investigation. It is not final results. The Defence's contention that what we did was reluctantly, hesitatingly beginning to investigate that is totally unwarranted. There contention that we obstructed their ability to bring out the truth is totally unwarranted. We acted appropriately in this instance, but Witness L's situation, this one Serb witness we had who said he saw crimes and then this issue arises, does not mean that rest of the Prosecution's case should be dismissed out of hand. The Defence has raised also this idea of a fair trial and have they been given a fair trial. They have not said it in those words, but at the beginning of trial certainly Mr. Wladimiroff raised the concern. He has raised it again about their inability to get all of the witnesses they wanted, the difficult conditions under which they worked. We suggest to you that they have not been denied a fair trial under this Statute. When it talks about the ability to obtain and present evidence what we are talking about is equality of arms, and in what way has the Prosecution or this Court acted to deprive them of opportunities that the Prosecution had? The fact that Prosecution witnesses many of them were not in Bosnian-Serb held territories does not constitute a denial of equality of arms. This Court went well beyond what many courts may have done to provide them with the opportunity to get witnesses to testify. So we suggest that there is no validity to this argument about a potential denial of a fair trial. They have also talked about the issue of corroboration. We suggest to you that, in fact, it is not uniform throughout civil law systems that corroboration is required in criminal trials. Germany, France, those systems do not require corroboration. This is an issue that this Tribunal, these Chambers, have obviously decided that they are going to be in line with the modern trend. If you as experienced jurists believe a single piece of information beyond a reasonable doubt, you may use that to convict. It is your assessment and your determination of the evidence that counts. Can you use corroboration as a factor? Certainly, always, and that is available to you, but it is not a legal requirement. There was something else that was raised in connection with 18 to 20, and that was that Defence counsel said that pertaining to 18 to 20 I had argued that you could base your findings on a reasonable inference and that in fact lowered the standard of proof. I believe that Defence counsel was talking about reference to reasonable belief that or reasonable inference that the victim was alive when the hose was shoved in the victim's mouth. I believe perhaps there are two issues here. As to the ability to use reasonable inferences from the evidence and use that as a basis to convict, I believe the law says you can do that as long as you are convinced beyond a reasonable doubt. But perhaps the issue there is, if there is more than one reasonable inference and the other reasonable inference is inconsistent with guilt, then of course that is a reasonable doubt. But it is not a matter of being able to rely on reasonable inferences. It is the matter of what is the one reasonable explanation you are left once you do the assessment. That, I believe, is the issue you face squarely on with 18 to 20, because the evidence there is very difficult evidence. It may very well be you find there is more than one reasonable inference and the other reasonable inference is inconsistent with guilt, but that is your determination to make based on the evidence and the reasonable inferences to be drawn from it. The Defence many times in their oral argument to you seemed to indicate that the Prosecution evidence should not be believed because it comes from those of the other party; not to be believed because it is based on sources that originated from the other party to the conflict; not to be believed because our evidence comes from victims of this persecution; only the other party was heard and subsequently called; solely based its case on witnesses of the other party. We suggest to you it is most unfortunate that the Defence has chosen to advance the same kind of thinking that led to this conflict, that people should be judged for the group they are assigned to rather than on an individual basis. In any violent crime may the fact-finder consider that a victim might have a prejudice? Yes, of course, just as you may believe that a victimizer might have a prejudice or a bias also to be untruthful. But that is an individual determination. It is unfortunate indeed that the Defence should urge you not to believe these people. Why is that? Because they had the great misfortune of being the victims of Serbs in opstina Prijedor, to be victimized and then to have it argued that victimization alone renders them unreliable to testify about what was done to them. That is a sad argument indeed. The Defence speculates that the Prosecution witnesses were willing, interested parties, quite willing to testify because they were motivated to talk. That is truly speculation. The Defence has no idea of the hesitation and fear, of the difficulties some of the witnesses had to come here to testify. The Defence has no idea of the number of potential witnesses who refused to come here to testify. That is speculation without any basis. If one considers the witnesses who appeared in this case, and you want to use a group analysis, we would suggest that you have on the one hand the victims and say, does that make them unbelievable, and, on the other hand, have members of a group that perhaps has a very strong motive to rewrite history to make the events in opstina Prijedor look less savage and less brutal. We urge upon you that you not fall into those kinds of group-based assessments of this evidence. This is not the evaluation you should be making. Going back to Witness S's remarks to you, you are here. It is time to break the tradition that he spoke of. Assess these individuals on both sides, the Prosecution and the Defence witnesses as individuals, and of course that is what you will do. Your Honours, let me assure you I am not playing to the Court when I tell you that you have dispensed justice throughout these proceedings, ruling in such a way as to give yourselves the most probative information available, but limiting the information to that which was probative for you. Please look carefully at the evidence that has been given to you, look at it in context. Look at the inconsistencies and determine if they are significant or minor, if they are the result of interpretation or translation errors, if they are the type of inconsistency you would expect from different people saying the same event and testifying to it later in time or if, in fact, the inconsistency is the product of intentional untruth. Once you have assessed this evidence and assigned it its proper weight, the weight of that evidence will lead you to the only reasonable conclusion that the accused's guilt has been proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any rejoinder, Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will just make a few remarks on the character of the conflict and I will also tried to look up the statement of Dr. Gow on the presence of JNA forces at the very end of his statement. What I found as a matter of fact is not the presence of JNA forces but, as Dr. Gow says, the shadow of the JNA being present in 1994 where some pilots of the VJ were flying aircraft. It is not very clear to me, but it is in a totally different time frame, as far as I understand. Then about Hambarine and the withdrawal of the JNA, here again we have the confusion, whether it is the 19th or 23rd. Whatever part of the JNA that remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina territory and that was not yet preparing or was already busy leaving, would have been regarded as the VRS because on from that moment the headquarters were changed from Sarajevo to the other place I cannot pronounce. When the Prosecutor refers to the resolution adopted on 30th May, I think it is was 757, I am not sure about the number, then I would draw your attention as well to the report of the Secretary General of that same day, although released perhaps a couple of hours later, where a totally different picture of the withdrawal of the JNA is made. I do not think that the Defence and the Prosecution are in disagreement on the wordings of the Nicaragua case, agent is acting on behalf of, but I emphasise the words prior to that phrase and those words are "such a degree of control in all fields as to justify treating the forces as acting on behalf". That is what I tried to find, whether there was such a degree of control in all fields in this case. The Prosecution has told me that I had overlooked Exhibit 180. I made a short remark on the testimony of Mr. Doko referring to that same Exhibit. Exhibit 180 clearly shows that there was a dispute between the President of the Serbian autonomous region of Herzegovina and the VJ about whether or not Podgorica Corps was withdrawing in an area east of Dubrovnik, which is far away from what we are talking about. It seems to be a rather isolated event, and it at least clearly indicates that there was great disagreement between the Serbian Herzegovinian autonomous region and Belgrade, which underlines again that Belgrade was not in control of what the Serbs did in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The last remark I will make on the absurdity of the outcome, Mr. Keegan when speaking on the Bosnian Serbs as protected persons under the Geneva Convention said that one must assume that the Appeals Chamber would find that they would have been protected persons as well, and he continues for the rest of his story, if that is the fact ... Well, it is not because the outcome is absurd because the Appeals Chamber did in fact find that the Bosnian Serbs would not be protected persons. So Mr. Keegan tells us that we have to read it this way, but that is core of the argument of the Appeals Chamber. The final remark is that it is not a matter of how a person considers their own citizenship as such, but whether they are nationals of a state because that is the element, whether they are nationals of one of the parties. Republika Srpska could not possibly be regarded as a state, as the Appeals Chamber learns us. Bosnian Serbs are presumed to hold Bosnia-Herzegovina citizenship which would prevent them from having the status of protected persons if the conflict would be international.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. We have come to the stage where the Prosecutor wants to have it both ways. When they speak, for example, about Witness H they say that he could not observe persons properly and suggest that, for this reason, he may not have observed Dusko Tadic who, as the Prosecution asserts, was there. But when it comes to other witnesses they say that floating glances, for example, are good enough to observe Dusko Tadic, and then they make references to the evidence of Professor Wagenaar. We may have done the same. So let us not continue this war of words, and only deal with the evidence. The evidence before you is clear and it is now for your Court to decide the case. So it is in your hands and let us not touch on it on any more. Your Honours, I will only make one final remark about identification since that issue seems to be very a important issue also in the eyes of the Prosecution. I will confine myself to three remarks, two in general, one in particular. The general remark is that, indeed, it has been explained to us over and over again that the only logical explanation is, as Professor Wagenaar told us, that when a witness recognises or better to say identifies an accused at the photospread the only logical explanation is that the accused was seen at the scene of the crime. Then the Prosecution puts a full stop. But we say unless the image of the accused was shown before or had been seen by the witness before, and that is the essence of the evidence of Professor Wagenaar, that you have to exclude the possibility that the witness saw the image of Dusko Tadic on another occasion. That is my first remark. Then I refer for all the details which have been presented by the Prosecution as well as for the Defence about what could have been known in public, and what is seen by witnesses or what has been read by witnesses. May I say this. Being a victim of the Bosnian conflict does not guarantee that one would not read about the Tadic case or would not watch TV in relation to Tadic. More specifically, being a Muslim victim of the suppression of the Serbs, being a Muslim victim who has been in the camps does not guarantee that such a victim would not be interested when a person accused of his oppression stands trial. It is in this context that we have reminded the Court that all four witnesses were tested by the photospread during the ongoing trial. My second remark in general is that you only can be certain about procedures if you would have received direct and complete evidence about it, but you have not. You have not heard evidence from Mr. Ackheim. You have not heard evidence from Mr. Safer. You have not been provided with their notes, if any. We only have the second-hand information of Mr. Reid. My final remark on this is more in detail and for that I will use two examples. First of all, Muslimovic. Indeed, I am not suggesting that he might have been a regular watcher of [redacted]. (redacted). But do keep in mind that before he emigrated [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: (redacted) to be exposed by information concerning Dusko Tadic. Your Honours, Draguna Jaskic, the point the Defence has made was not that she has been shown the photospread twice. The point we have made is that Professor Wagenaar was very clear about his assessment that her statement does not include a positive identification. Therefore, she is not one of the four positive identification witnesses. When it comes to Mr. Paepen who was involved in this matter, we stress that there is no evidence that he ever performed a photospread before, a photospread test before. It may be that I am more careful in listening to language than others because I am not a native speaker, but the Prosecution during commenting on this aspect did not even suggest that he ever did. Finally, your Honour, dealing with interpretation and translation, in Court we have had simultaneous interpretation. The prior statements to which we referred were read back to the witness. So, if we have problems in Court, we have told you that these were of a minor importance. "Wheelbarrow" or "wheelchair" does not bear any importance on the substance of the evidence. Let me close, your Honours, with the speculations about the way we dismantled this pack of lies of witness L. The assertions of the Prosecution about this are totally unfounded, as are the allegations about Pero Opacic. It is highly unfair to make that statement without proper evidence. Let us only realise what the witness L story really means. It means that we cannot simply rely on evidence given in Court by witnesses, and that is what this case is all about. Specifically when the evidence of both sides, your Honour, let us face it, may be divided by ethnical lines, we trust and we are convinced that this Court will find that the evidence presented by both parties will not satisfy that Dusko Tadic is guilty of any of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wladimiroff. Does that conclude the Defence rejoinder?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Let me sign this last redaction here. I did want to make just a few remarks, if I may? Probably, as the participants know, it is over six months ago that we began this trial. We have heard from over 120 witnesses and I do not know how many exhibits we have received into evidence, but I understand that we have over 6,000 pages of transcript. So I wanted on behalf of Judge Stephen and Judge Vohrah and, of course, myself to thank the participants for their very professional behaviour. May I say participants, it is participants in this courtroom, but it is participants in the booths and in places that you really cannot see. It is really with their assistance that we have been able to proceed as we have. I think that the legal representation, as we said previously, has been absolutely outstanding and that makes a Judge's job much easier. So I want to thank the lawyers as well on behalf of Judge Stephen, Judge Vohrah and myself. This is the first trial before the International Tribunal and, as I said, we have over 6,000 pages of transcript. We have read many of the pages of transcript ourselves, if not all of them, already but I am sure that we will review them again, we will look at all of the evidence and we will render a judgment in due course. So the Court is adjourned. 1.05 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: (The Court adjourned for a short time)
